Admiral Hawkins, of the Royal British Navy, adopted a good plan to rid his command of the reproach of þÿ profane swearing on board which that useless indulgence, of his ships: brings no present or after enjoyment with it, and is the sure criterion of a lack of gentlemanlike qualities, to say nothing of morality and religion. Hawkins was a religious man himself, and he endeavored to encourage in his people those religious feelings which they had rather disregarded than despised ; and after they had solemnly returned thanks to God for their deliverance when the ship was on fire and in imminent danger of being consumed, he took occasion, with their general consent, " to banish swearing out of the three ships." This ! was effected by ordaining that in every | ship there should be a ferule given to I the first who was "taken with an oath," ; He could be rid of it only by taking another in the same offence, when he was to give him a stroke on the palm, and transfer to him the instrument of punishment. Whoever had it in his possession at the time of morning or evening prayer was to receive three blows Iroin the captain, or master, and sull bear it, till he could make a transfer agreeable to the law. This, in a few days, brought both swearing and " ferules out of use. We copy the following from u The St. Christopher Gazette f of 31st December : þÿ

We have been favored with the perusal of a letter received by a gentleman of this Town, from his correspondent at St. Thomas. From this source we learn that great and praiseworthy endeavors have been made by our neighbors, at the instance of His Majesty of Denmark, to ameliorate their present position, and to adapt their Laws to the altered state of things. We learn that the Danish Government have appointed a Colonial Council for her West India possessions, for the purpose of revising their Laws, and framing such new Ordinances as may be deemed essential to the well working of their present enlightened system This Council was composed oft) Members from St. Thomas, 8 from St. Croix, 2 from St. J ohns, and 4 Nominees of the Crown, making in all a Council of 20. For two months this well devised Representative Body have been sedulously and ably engaged in their work of Legislation. Their labors have terminated, and only await the necessary confirmation of His Majesty to form a code of Laws, well calculated, to benefit all classes concerned. We trust soon to learn that such a code, so long required, and so carefully framed by a Council so judiciously composed, has received vitality. Doubtless the Colonial Advisers of Ilis Majesty, will strongly urge the Executive sanction of Laws so wisely originated. Sad indeed, will be the result, if after so great a sacrifice of time, money and personal convenience, on the part of the gentlemen composing this Council, the Colonists should find their labor

rendered abortive by the imposition of the Royal veto. We cannot anticipate a disaster so fatal to any future Legislative effort, in the like well directed channel. We heartily congratulate our Danish neighbors on their progress in Representative Legislation, and we wish them Goodspeed

The Colonial Council have the honor to make this most submissive report on the draft of an ordinance to prevent vagrancy in the Danish Westimfia Possessions. The Council deem it their duty generally to observe, that the existing Danish legislation relative to vagrancy seems to have especially in view, the prevention of those practices with which persons without occupation endanger the public security; whereas the relations in the Westindia Islands demand, that the principal object of such a law shall be, to counteract vagrancy, which is an evil, that threatens the whole community with dissolution. From the nature of the climate the manner of livelihood and the propensities of the poorer classes, many individuals are able to procure their sustenance by trifling and casual work, or by dwelling with or importuning others just as poor, and existing only by the productions of nature, without being forced by want to commit actual crime, and without being obliged to apply for relief from the poor institution. Such an undisturbed indolent state, without interference by or responsibility with regard to others, þÿ which in itself is, and leads to the contrary of European and anglo-American industry, þÿ is thus to that degree the greatest happiness for a number of persons, that it often is the only condition, which the parents of the lower classes try to secure to their

children. This tendency to inactivity is far stronger than any inclination to vice ; it counteracts þÿ and that not always by passive opposition only þÿ the public as well as private efficacy in the promotion of the population towards european civilisation, it undermines the prosperity

of the islands, and in addition thereto also that condition that leads to that prosperity. It is therefore certainly right, that the draft contains provisions according to which admonition to seek lawful maintenance is to be given as well as assignment of work, and in case of disobedience punishment for vagrancy is to be inflicted on all persons, whose condition of life does not afford any guarantee, that they support themselves without detriment to the public. The sphere of action assigned to the police is so of extensive with the number individuals on whom the regard to law is applicable, that there is rather to be dreaded a relaxation than an abuse of such a power. The local regulations existing heretofore regarding vagrancy have in general been but slightly maintained ; therefore the number of persons without fixed livelihood as well as the comparatively great number for als, who are unqualified of individu- regular work, or whose services, nobody will have, inevitably demand many restrictions respecting them. Hence it becomes a question of importance: if it is proper so short a time after the emancipation completely to do away with all the preventative or controlling regulations, which have hitherto existed (the last ordained by Governþÿment circular s of 29th September 1849;) þÿ certain it is, that through the means of these regulations, numerous thoughtless removals into the towns and the consequent results thereof, both as regards the cultivation of the country and

the respective parties themselves, have been prevented ; þÿ many estate laborers have meanwhile learnt to appreciate their comparatively good condition, especially in St. Croix. But besides the temptations held out a to the younger people to enter into visionary independence in the towns (often only a nominal situation as servants,) the town of St. Thomas, on account of its peculiar relations offers inducements and opportunities to seek their fortune there ; and those individuals, who have once left their situation in the country do not return, and when they do, they are either unfit or corrupted. YVe will however return hereafter to this subject when treating on the proposed amendment to at paragraph As it meanwhile any rate must be G. admitted, that the law before us is of a very forcible and extensive nature, we must be very cautious with regard to the means we intend to adopt in the execution of such laws. As far as the police-authorities are not provided with a particular respectability and independence, and besides are sufliciently controlled with respect to the execution of their authority, both as administrative and judicial officials, there is scarcely any doubt, but that unfortunate results will arise. THE FRENCH EMPIRE. The Senate and Corps Legislatif went on Wednesday evening to St. Cloud, to present the Empire to Louis Napoleon. Having presented the result of the voting, they were thus addressed by the Emperor : Gentlemen, þÿ The new reign which you this day inaugurate derives its origin þÿ not as so many others recorded in history have done, from violence, from conquest, or from fraud. It is as you have just declared, the legal result of the will of an entire peo- ! ple, who consolidate in calm that which they had founded in the midst of agitation. I am penetrated with gratitude to the nation which, three times in four years, has sustained me by its suffrages, and each time has only augmented its majority to increase my power. But the more that power increases in extent and in vital force, the more does it need enlightened men, such as those who every day surround me þÿ independent men, such as those whom I addressþÿ to guide me by their counsel, to bring back my authority within just limits, if it ever could quit them. From this day forward I take, with the crown, the name of þÿ Napoleon þÿIII., because it is that which the logic of the people has bestowed upon me in their acclamations ; because the senate has legally proposed it ; and because the whole nation has ratified it. Is it then to be inferred that in accepting this title I fall into the error imputed to the Prince who, returning from exile, declared null and void all that had been done in his absence ? Far from me j

be such a wild mistake. Not only do I recognise the governments which have preceded me, but I inherit in some manner all that they have accomplished of good and evil ; for governments which succeed one to another are, notwithstanding different origin, liable for their predecessors. But the more completely that I accept all that for fifty years history transmits to us with her inflexible authority, the less is it permitted to me to pass in silence over the glorious reign of the head of my family, and the regular, though ephemeral, title of his son, whom the two Chambers proclaimed in the last burst of vanquished patriotism. Thus, then, the title of Napoleon III. is not one of those dynastic and superannuated pretensions which seem to be an insult to good sense and to truth. It is the homage due to a government which was legitimate, and to which we owe the brightest pages of our modern history. My reign does not date from 1815þÿ it dates from this very moment when you have announced to me the suffrages of the nation. Receive, then, my thanks, Messieurs Its Deputies, for the eclat that you have given to the manifestation of the national will by rendering it more evident by your supervision, more imposing by your declaration. I thank you also, Messieurs Its Semteurs, for having been the first to address congratulations to me, as you were the first to give expression to the popular wish. Aid me, then, all of you, to set firm in this land, upset by so many revolutions, a stable Government, j neatly

which shall have for its basis religion, probity, and love for the suffering classes. Receive here my oath, that no sacrifice shall bo wanting on my part to insure the prosperity of my country ; and that, whilst I maintain peace, I will yield in nothing which may concern the honour or the dignity of France

£J» We make the following extract from the report of the directors of the þÿ North of Europe Steam Navigation þÿCompany, þÿ Morning þÿHerald published in the London of December 10. þÿ The trade with Denmark via Lowestoft is one, although new, of so important and extensive a character, and probably so little understood by the majority of our friends, that we think it advisable, even at the risk of trespassing on their time, to enter more fully into detail. þÿ The repeal of the import duties on cattle opened a new era in the import trade of this country, which has been greatly aided by the increased means at the disposal of the working classes for the purchase of animal food. The fanners and graziers of Schleswig-Holstein, and Jutland, on whose rich marshes upwards of 40.000 head of cattle are fatted and exported annually, naturally turned their attention to the English market. A trial was made in 1848, with questionable success, on account of the inferior character of the steamers employed ; for it haB taken experience to establish what common sense should at first have dictated, that to carry a cargo of live cattle, with perfect safety and expedition, across the German Ocean in all weathers, would require the best and steadiest ships that could possibly be procured. But a commencement once made was soon improved upon. In 1850 upwards of 8000 head were exported from Tonning to London ; in 1851 it had increased to 12.000 and this year, from June to November, , nearly 20,000 head of oxen had been exported

from that port to London þÿ Of these oxen, as before stated, no less than 10,742 have been brought by the ships of the Northern Steam-packet Company into Lowestoft, and conveyed by rail to London, for the Smitbfield market. þÿ When it is considered that 20,000 oxen will be 100 freights for large steamers þÿ that it is of the last importance they should be conveyed in the least possible time by the nearest sea voyage, and in the shortest space, and if so conveyed must always secure a remunerative freight þÿ this alone forms the nucleus of a very large and permanent trade, which has been greatly enhanced by the success that has attended, during the past year, the importation into Lowestoft, which, by shortening the sea voyage, has very much lessened the risk ; in proof of which, the City of Norwich (a ship built expressly for this trade by the Northern Steam Packet Company, and now our property) has in 15 weeks, performed 15 voyages to Tonning and back, bringing near 4000 head of oxen, and as many sheep, without the loss of a single head ! þÿ Nor is this all A glance at the map of ! Denmark will show that the extensive peninsula of Schleswig and Jutland is only 35 miles across between the important port of Tonning on the Eider, and the equally important port of Flensborg on the Baltic. Across this isthmus, Mr. Peto, your deputy chairman, obtained this summer a full concession from the King of Denmark to make a line of railroad without restriction. Since then the line has been surveyed, the work

has actually been commenced, and it is fully expected that a large portion will be open for traffic by the autumn of next year þÿ When we consider that this short link will connect the Baltic with the German Oceanþÿ that it will place the important capital of Copenhagen within 48 hours of London þÿ that it will open the door to the Baltic Sea, without enduring the lengthened, dangerous, and intricate navigation of the Sound and Bolt þÿ that it will, in short, save 300 miles of sea voyage to Copenhagen, 500 to Flensborg and the southern parts of Denmark, as well as be a shorter and safer route to Sweden, Stettin, Riga, St. Petcrsburgh, and every part of he Baltic þÿ its advantages cannot be overrated.

3 U\ S ift « 1Z 4?J , It is, in fact, as important to these countries as a railway across the Isthmus of Suez is to India, or that of Panama to the western coast of America and the Pacific. þÿ The port of Flensborg is one of the finest and safest in the world. Already its trade is of considerable extent, not only coastways, and to various ports of the Baltic, but also to the West Indies, the intercourse with which is greatly retarded by the long and tedious navigation of the Cattegat and Belts, but which the connection by rail with Tonning will obviate, and enable their vessels to perform two voyages to one. þÿ Simultaneously with this, the proprietors of the Copenhagen and Roeskilde Railway have determined to continue their line to Korsoer, a port on the west coast of Zealand, and only 65 miles from Flensborg, thereby opening the richest and most important island of Denmark, as well as the capital, by an easy run in smooth water of five or six hours to Flensborg. þÿ This alone is a great acquisition to an intercourse with this country, not only as regards passengers, but the produce of the eastern coast and fertile islands of Denmark, from which country upwards of a million of quarters of grain are annually exported, as well as large quantities of butter and other produce, whilst the increased facility and cheapness of transit will convey to them our raw material and manufactures direct, without the circuitous and expensive method of their present indirect routes. þÿ The port of Tonning being reached from

London via Lowestoft in thirty hours, an easy ride of two hours will convey passengers or goods to Flensborg, on the shores of the Baltic. A run of five hours by sea, and four more by rail, will reach Copenhagen þÿ or forty-one hours, say (stoppages included) forty-four hours. This is the time now occupied, via Ostcnd, to reach Hamburgh by rail, and only two thirds of the average passage by sea, and less than half the average passage by any existing route to Copenhagen. And the same holds good respecting all places in the Baltic, either in Sweden, Germany, or Russia, now reached by the Cattegat and Sound . þÿ We feel assured we need not further refer to this portion of our service than to recommend the study of this important country to our friends, so essential is an agricultural and producing district to the increasing wants of this country. þÿ The next route it is thought advisable to open out, in the same ensuing year, is a direct and weekly communication with Norway and Sweden, by sea. þÿ It will be seen that these countries lie too far north to avail themselves of the overland route pointed out to Flensborg ; and as railway influence is also opening out the resources of their country, their demand for direct communication with England becomes more urgent. To encourage this, the government of Sweden have granted the sum of 2000/. per annum for a weekly communication between this country and Gottenburgh, calling, if required, at Christiansand, in Norway. Although this is a very small sum, as

a contract for carrying a mail, yet, as it was intended to run to those countries, it was thought more desirable to run with this bonus than without it, especially as the contract embraced certain privileges highly advantageous to this company. This contract has, therefore, been taken by your directors for five years ; and they propose, as early as possible, to construct two screw-steamers, of moderate power and good capacity, in order to carry out the same in a satisfactory as well as profitable þÿmanner.

Orders have just been issued for the enlistment of 2,000 additional artillerymen, and for the purchase oil, 000 horses, which are to be exclusively appropriated to this branch of the service. Nor is this all. Vigorous measures are in progress for the construction of so many carriages and ammunition waggons as may be requisite for 200 field guns. At the present rate of preparation these batteries will be ready for service by the latter end of winter, or early in the spring; but if any greater expedition were necessary, the time of preparation could be very materially shortened. þÿ The Times. It is likely that our suggestion for making the 5,000 men proposed this year as a reserve for the navy, will be added to the regular force of seamen for 1853-4, and we hear that the vote for steam machinery will be comparatively enormous. During the last two or three years a vote only of £50,000 has been taken for steam machinery, a sum of money utterly inadequate to the wants of the navy; but we believe that, awake to the requirements of the service, no less a sum than £380,000 will be demanded by the government for steam machinery alone, to restore the Royal Navy to its proper position. An increased vote for timber and stores, and for placing our steam establishments in efficient working order, we trust, will likewise be included in the demands for 1853-4. þÿ Morning Herald. Orders have recently been issued to hasten the preparations for commencing the construction of the batteries in the

Isle of Wight, and to expedite the works as fast as possible. þÿ Ministerial Paper. Increase of the Royal Marine Forces. We understand that it is proposed in the new estimates to add to the present strength of the Royal Marines 1,500 men. The Estimates. It is said that the increase to the army, in personal and material, will include an addition to the artillery branch of 2,000 men, 1,000 horses and carriages, and ammunition waggons for 200 guns. þÿ Ministerial Paper.

Dench, yesterday week, before Lord j Campbell and a special jury, Lord Frankj fort was indicted for conspiring to defame the character of Lord Henry Lennox, by causing to be circulated libellous writings. Letters of a very peculiar description, alleged to be written by the defendant, were circulated through the j Post-office and other channels, in which the name of the prosecutor was most unpleasantly used They purported to effect interviews with ladies of distinction and position, and that several assignations of a very favourable character j had been accomplished through the source employed. Inspector Field and Sergeant Thornton, of the detective force, traced the writings to the defendant, who held out a threat to them that he would have them punished. The jury found the defendant guilty. Lord Campbell said lie quite agreed in the verdict, and the sentence he felt bound to inflict was that he be imprisoned in the House of Correction for the space of twelve months. Lord Frankfort was j his þÿlordship custody. removed in s arrival at the House of Immediately on Correction he was placed in the cells used for the reception of ordinary prisoners. On Saturday morning bis lordship, having gone through the ceremony ot the hath, was clad in the prison apparel, and his own clothing taken from him He appeared lo feel the degradation of his position most acutely. His lordship, will not being sentenced to hard labour, be exempted from the task of the tread-wheel and oakum-picking,
providing lie pays a sum of five shillings weekly for the cost of his support.

Munificence of Louis Napoleon at Fontainebleau. The Prince President, when at Fontainebleau, visited the hospital, the house of the sisters of Charity, and the Orphan Asylum. In each he left marks of his munificence. The Prince was accompanied by the prefect of the Seine-ct-Marine, the sub-prefect of the town, and the mayor. The Prince afterwards visited the church, and was much struck by its small size, and its want of repair. The mayor and the Cure told the Prince that the town ardently desired to see a new and larger church constructed, but that funds were wanting. The Prince reminded them that he was christened at Fontainebleau, ; and promised to give 200,000 f. from his own purse, towards a fund for a new church He subsequently charged M. Blouet, architect of the palace, to draw up a plan of the church. When the generosity of the Prince became known it excited great enthusiasm amongst the population.

Remittances from Irish settlers in Australia are steadily increasing, and there is every likelihood that the supplies from this source will before very long, equal the sums trans- A Nobleman Sent to the House of i milted from the United Slates. The inevita- In the Court of þÿQueen s ble effect must be to stimulate emigrants to Australia lo a very great extent; and, from present appearances, it is most probable that the exodus will proceed upon an enormous scale next spring. Lately seventy registered money letters, sent by Irish emigrants at Melbourne, were received at the Limerick post office, with sums ranging from £50 to ! £500. The writers, in almost all cases, gave the most encouraging accounts of the prospects in this colony, and held out strong inducements to their friends to join them. The American remittances, although of immense amount in the aggregate, have generally consisted of small sums, averaging from £3 to £20. þÿ Boston Pilot.

The filthy state of the public sewers, is and oilier places where dung collected, is very much in town com plained of also. Although we cannot complain, to that extent, of similar evils existing here; yet we would invite the Police, to turn their attention to those places here in town, where dung is collected, lor the sale, or for own use. These dungheaps purpose of preparing manure either for j in the letter, sorry are generally in large open yards, bordering on the sea; yea, even in the very centre of the town. There is a lot, belonging to the public, in Strand Street, in the immediate neighbourhood of dwellings, where this nuisance exists and where the contents of privies are sometimes emptied. The undersigned inhabitants of St. Thomas, take the liberty to supplicate Your Honorable Board, to take into consideration, the sanitary state of our island, ami provide the measures, which are available, in order to stay the evil, or at least to prevent a further increase of the same. A fearful malady has for the last three months been decimating the crews of our merchant vessels, without any hospital or other proper abode being up pro pi iated by the Authorities, to receive such sick persons. On the contrary, our town is filled, almost house by house, with sick and dying, and it is greatly to he feared, that the malady may lie brought in amongst our population, if it still continues much longer, and Government does not supply a place, out of l lie immediate centre of the town, where sick people can In carried to, wi (limit risk to the inhabitants. It is, likewise, much to In regretted, that no notice whatever is taken of the swamp to the east of the town, which could he laid dry with li'tle expense, nor of the horribly filthy state of our sewers, from which the most pestilential evaporations are emanating ; the same as is the case with the almost innumerable dunghills all about town, from which of necessity must arise the most prejudicial miasmata, to the detriment of the general health of our densely populated town. It is, because, we see no notice whatever taken of these matters, of so great importance in a sanitary point of view, that we take the liberty to address Your

In our paper of the 14th instant, we published some remarks on the treatment of the \ ellow Fever, from Doctor Robert Thomas's work on the modern practice of Physic. We now beg leave to offer our readers the following extract, from the same work, containing some hints, by an attention to which, as the author asserts, Europeans may often be enabled to withstand the attack of the Yellow Fever ; or if seized, to go through it with the least danger subjects þÿ The plethoric and to robust most liable this malignant being the disease, all such, on their approach to the warm latitudes, ought to lie bled in proportion been this have to their strength ; lint should neglected during the voyage, it may he done immediately on their arrival on shore. It will easily lie understood here, that bleeding, as a preparative, will have very a different effect from what it would have in a curative intention; for in the former, it prevents morbid action, and gives time for assimila-

tion ; whereas, in the latter, it may induce debility and n.orbid association, very dangerous to life. After bleeding, if the patient is of a full and plethoric habit, the bowels are to he opened by some cooling purgative ; and if he is naturally of a bilious habit, it may he advisable to premise a gentle emetic. Having adopted these steps, lie may then begin a slight course of mercury, taking from two to four grains of hydrargyri suhmurias, according to his age and other circumstances, every other night, either in the form of a pill, or that of a powder, mixed in some thick vehicle, until the gums become somewhat affected. Should the medicine run through the bowels, a grain of opium, or a few drops of tinctura opii, may be added to each dose. When the mouth shows the mercurial action, a do3e oi some cooling laxative ought to be administered after one or two þÿdays intermission of the medicine. In some constitutions, not easily affected by mercury, it will he necessary to persevere with steadiness, until the system be thoroughly impregnated ; for thereon depends the safety of the patient. On his voyage being completed, and his landing, he must observe the greatest temperance in his diet, and carefully guard against any exposure to the sun in the middle of the day, and to t lie cool air of the night, until he becomes somewhat habituated to t lie climate. The effects of temperance, as a prophylactic, are strikingly demonstrated by Dr. Cliisliolme, who observes, that while the

yellow fever raged at die island of Grenada, the utility of this was remarkably illustrated by the almost total exemption of the French inhabitants from the disease, whose mode of living, compared with that of the English, is temperate and regular in an uncommon degree. Or. CliirUc lei la us, that new settlers who could he prevailed upon to undergo a gentle course of mercury, taking a few laxative medicines, afterwards confining themselves to a moderate use of wine, and living chiefly on vegetables and fruits for the first two or three months, may rely almost to a certainty on escaping this fever. The remark is, I think, well founded, excepting that, notwithstanding all these precautions, it may arise from contagion ; and in this case its virulence, in all probability, will be greatly diminished. priority Europeans appear of and severity to suffer in point ol attack by the yellow fever, precisely in the degree that they possess bodily vigour, rigidity of fibre, and are of a sanguineous temperament; and when relaxed by a long residence, or other causes, they become, like the creoles and people of colour (as they are termed,) in a great degree exempt from the influence of this fever. It is the reduction ot tone, which a certain period of residence occasions in the constitution of Europeans, that secures them in a great measure from the seizure of the yellow fever. It is a corresponding (atonic) state of constitution which affords immunity to the native inhabitþÿant.

From the London Times, November 10. The Yellow Fercr. TO THE EDITOR OF THE TIMES. þÿSts, Perceiving that the yellow fever i still committing its ravages among the troops, at Barbados, ami having had some experience of that disease, I beg to make a few remarks on a matter which has not yet received the attention due to it from the authorities, if indeed it has ever been brought under their notice. I am sure that any surgeon who has had charge of soldiers during a severe epidemic can call to mindmany cases in which the disease has been subdued by treatment or the constitution of the patient, and yet h has sunk þÿ þÿexhausted, as it is termed. In private life, in all huinau probability, the þÿman s life would

have been saved, and how is t that he dies in a military hospital, which, I ani proud to say, is generally an example of all that skill and regularity can effect 'I It is because he wants that nursing which none but women understand, and none but wonvn can execute. þÿMen natures s are too rugged (be they ever so well inclined) to smooth the sick man's pillow, to watch bis every look, and to minister to his wants, at the right time and in the right way. I am quite certain that 1 owe my life, under I'rovidence, to the careful nursing of a black woman during an attack of yellow fever, and 1 am anxious that every soldier should have the same advantage. I would therefore propose, that in addition to the usual number of hospital orderlies, black women should be hired to attend the fever patients in the proportion of one nurse to four men. A most important reason for this measure is, that all risk of the disease spreading from the sick soldier to his comrade nurse would be avoided, and, though a noncontagionist, I am of opinion that we cannot be too cautious. Any remarks on treatment would be out of place here ; but I must congratulate the service on ol tire promptitude with which that most important all measures þÿ placing the men under canvas, has been carried out, and, in conclusion, would suggest that the way to treat, yellow fever in liarbadoes is to raze to the ground the whole of the barracks at St. þÿAnne s, and with the materials build new ones at Gunhill, an elevated and most healthy spot seven miles from Bridge-

town, and whence, as it is a telegraph station, the troops could always be brought in a couple ol hours. I need only allude to the condition ol the white troops at Jamaica to prove ho'Jf healthy they have been since they have b'een placed at the mountain stations of Newcastle and Maroontown. I am, Sir, your most obedient servant, A MEDICAL OFFICER. London, Nov. 8.

Treatment. þÿ Administer a good dose of caster oil, and put the feet into a very hot foot hath about half tin hour sifter taking the oil, to cresite perspiration. A HILL opposed to, and rejecting of, all measures having for object, the sale, transfer, and consequent separation of the Danish West India Possessions from the Parent State. ls< Session. 1( Silling. Whereas : Certain statements published in the Danish papers of Copenhagen announced the ataccording to the Danish þÿ( ode, s ;ats, in the Diet, to express their sentiments in tempts made to induce some of the candidates for favor of, or pledge themselves to, vole for measures having for object the sale, transfer, and consequent separation of the Danish West India Possessions from the Parent State

Considering : That the circulation of such statements, in D nmark, can have no good tendency, but to the contrary, create unfavorable impressions at variance with the natural sentiments of loyaltv and confidence, which the Inhabitants of these Islands cherish for their Government. Considering : That the solemn expression of the popular will and sentiments are known by the proceedings of the Agents, whom the people appoint to represent their will. Resolved : That the Representatives of the Danish subjects in these Colonies, deem it necessary to record their sentiments, in regard of the statements alluded. Therefore declare, all project or proposition to þÿ 2lsr rent State, either sale or alienate any portion of these Islands from the Pa- by transfer, unjust and inadmissible, and affording palpable evidence of the ignorance and evil design of the parties, inasmuch as they, wilfully, pretend to ignore the instinct and patriotism of the colonists þÿ their unalterable attachment and fidelity to their Sovereign, Laws and Government ; and their firm determination to uphold, unimpaired and indivisible, the national tie by which they are bound to Denmark as Danish Subjects. Resolved : That with the view of explaining the facts stated to our fellow citizens, this House recommend and request, that His Excellency the Governor will he pleased to cause a copy of these proceedings to be published in the leading journals in the Danish Capital. Council Hall. Signed, Jos. De Gout.

The Mover of the Bill having introduced the subject by some preliminary remarks, the House expressed its approbation and to unanimously e 1 that it should be referred a Committee, con- resolvsisting of three members, who have subsequently presented the following Report, which was also adopted. REPORT. The undersigned Committee, appointed to repert on the memorial from the 3d member for St. Thomas district , that the Colonial Council would forwa'd a most submissive representation to His Maresty the King, protesting against the question which has been started by some members of the D'.et, relative to the sale of those colonies, which question has been taken up by some of the Cop nhagen voters, who have made it an object of interpellation at the Poll. The proposal moved at the Diet was rejected, consequently, the expressions that passed at the Poll must be considered as null. We hav" not the most distant cause to suppose, that His Majesty or His þÿMajesty Government s would have any idea whatever to propose such a sale, or to consider any such proposal, should it ever be repeated. We are fully convinced, that the Danish Government at no period would cherish the idea of making about 40,000 individuals an object of purchase and sale, persons who, with but a few exceptions, have perfect claim to Danish citizenship, according to the laws regarding the rights of nativity, and out of which a number of others have domiciled themselves here, and partly invested their capital with the full faith in the protec-

tion of the laws and the Danish Government. We are, moreover, less disposed to adopt and repel, the thought, considering, that His Majesty by giving to these Islands the Colonial Council, to whom we have the honor of making this our report, 1 as thus off'red an acknowledgment of the privilege of the Inhabitants to express their opinion in all matters regarding their interests. We would, therefore, dismiss the idea of any sale, on which subject we do not consider an address to His Majesty is at this moment expedient, a step which implying a doubt would-be in our estimation as offensive as it would be without reason. We, therefore, only propose and now recommend that the object of the mover be furthered thus, that the Council would, through the means of His þÿMajesty Representative s the Governor of these Islands, express that firm hope and unshaken conviction cherished by the inhabitants of the Danish Colonies ; that His Majesty will be graciously pleased, never to listen to any proposition, if it should ever bo discussed, of the transfer by sale or otherwise of these Islands. Christianstcd, 8th November 1852. Jos. De Gout. Bnhnebcrg. II. L. Arntstn.

That want of respect for the Authorities, and particularly for the Police, of which some of the lowest class of the inhabitants of this town, have repeatedly given examples, has, on Christmas-Eve last, caused a melancholy catastrophe, of which we, with the profoundest regret, have to inform our readers. the Christmas Season in amusements, which, spends A part of these people, as is well known, partly, consist in parading through the streets with a kind of noisy, discordant music and singing ; and, partly, in dancing. As we have learned, the case does not stand as some have supposed, that the Police had prevented these processions through the streets ; but it was fixed as a rule, with regard to the places where these dances could be continued, in accordance with an order from the Government, that the so-called Gumbee dances should not be held in such places in the town, where it might be supposed, that the neighbours would be disturbed by the noise ; neither in such places wherefrom complaints, on this point, were made. In a house or yard, situated about the middle of the town, by the Sunday market, they had already, on the day before Christmas-Eve, yea even for many days previous, begun with Gumbee drumming, and on these persons being called up at the Police Office, they were informed, that they should choose some other place in the outskirts of the town for this purpose, while, on the other hand, it was plainly intimated to them that no objection was held to the processions through the

streets. Notwithstanding this, the Gumbee dance commenced at the same place on Christmas-Eve, which caused the Police to appear on the spot, and as no one owned himself to be the owner of the drum, the skin of the same was immediately cut, and the noise thus in this usual and practical manner stopped. Some hours after, about 10 þÿo clock, as the Police patrolled the streets, while the processions undisturbed went along the streets with all sorts of music, it was discovered that the drum-dance had again commenced in this same place. Accordingly, the Police again repaired to the spot, and the place was immediately vacated by all present. As the Police- Servants came out in the street from this place, they were assaulted with stones thrown at them, and were obliged, after two of them had been rather severely wounded, to retire to the Police Office, the gate of which, luckily, was hastily closed by the Police-servant there on duty, after the other Police-servants had come insido, so that the mass could not force in ; which precaution prevented what would, without doubt, have taken place, viz: the destruction of the Archives and Protocols of the Island, in the same manner as took place in Frederiksted on the 3d July 1848 This large mass of people, which remained outside the Police Office, and which, at the same time, must have swelled larger by the accession of others, who formed part of the processions, then threw at the building a quantity of stones of great size, until Military assistance arrived, when they gave way

In one of the hy-strects, by the Catholic Church, a military patrol was assaulted by a shower of stones, and after a few shots had been fired in the air, without intimidating the mob, who still continued to throw stones with renewed vigor ; and as some of the soldiers (we are told 8) were

wounded by the stones, the command was given to fire, from the effects of which, according to the information that we have been able to obtain, 1 man fell dead on the spot, 1 man and a woman were wounded in such a manner that they died on the following morning at the Hospital, and seven other persons were, more or less, dangerously wounded. The same excited tone, however, still pervaded the mass, and outside the Government- House a patrole, being under an attack with stones, was obliged to fire, by which, however, as far as we know, no one was wounded. After this the different gatherings kept at long distances, wherever the patrols showed themselves, and by one þÿo clock in the following mo.ning there were no others to be seen on the streets but the Military and the Police. During the tumult were heard exhortations from the women to the men ; that they should hasten for their muskets, and two militia drummers even began to roll their drums, who were, however, quickly silenced by those present. The following morning at 6 þÿo clock, it was perceived that the Militia officers were summoned to appear at the Government- House, where the Government officials and the commander of the military forces, along with some other officers were previously gathered together until 3 o'clock in the morning. At the command of Ilis Excellency the Governor, three divisions, consisting of a couple of militia officers, 1 officer of the royal troops and a detachment of soldiers and troopers, (which last had before dawn of dry been sum-

moned to the town from the military station at Kingshill,) likewise an officer of the Police, proceeded to the different quarters of the town and received the arms from each member of the militia corps singly, at their residences. By ten þÿo clock all the muskets were deposited in the fort. We cannot but repeat the call to tire Inhabitants of this town, contained in the proclamation of the Government, which we, judging from the general quiet which, since this occurrence, has reigned in the town, believe to have had the desired effect ; as likewise we must state that the precautionary measures taken, seem to have met with approving acknowledgment from the welldisposed inhabitants of all classes. It is certainly sorrowful that human life should be sacrificed on such an occasion as this ; but it was to be expected that that particular class of the inhabitants of our town, sooner or later, might learn, that neither the Authorities nor the Military force can be insulted and attacked without serious consequences.

TRANSLATION. PROCLAMATION TO THE Inhabitants of Christianstcd. It is with the deepest pain, that I have seen the peace of the town disturbed by disorders, which have been carried into attacks on tho public force, and thereby led even to bloodshed and tiie los3 of human life All faithful subjects must acknowledge, that public authority must be obeyed, and that attacks on the officials or on the military force must be quelled by tho means disponible in such cases. Whether any individual may have used his arms beyond the necessity of the case will, without delay, be made the subject of legal investigation. First of all public peace must be maintained. In order to prevent the danger to the peace, which might arise, if Arms of tha Militia now kept in privato houses should fall into the hands of evil-minded and seditious persons, I have caused the said arms to bo deposited in tho Fort, in order to be delivered from there to the proper parties', whenever tho Militia bo called out. The processions in the streets, which have been customary during tho Holydays, and all other assemblages in the streets or other public places, are hereby prohibited until further.

Inhabitants of Christiansted 1 In the name of His Majesty the King I do hereby call upon you to support me in the preservation of the peace in the town and throughout the Island. Let the Victims of this first violation of the public Peace during my Government bo a warning and an inducement to prevent the recurrence of any such deplorable events. Government-House, St. Croix 25th December 1852. FEDDERSEN.

Now that the year 1852 is hastening to a close, and we are fast entering upon another year, we beg to say a few words, which, we hope, may not he out of place. We have, þÿ tis true, during the year that will in a few hours b, closed, been tried with many severe afflictions, and within the past few months death has been very busy among us; but still, in the midst of all this, we have enjoyed many happy moments ; and what is most worthy of our notice, we have experienced one of the greatest favors of our beloved Sovereign þÿ the Colonial Council ; the members of which, we are confident, will do every thing in their power, to meet the wants ol the people, and assist the Government in framing sound and equitable laws. We have had very lately, only last week, to deplore the loss of the lives of a few unfortunate and misguided persons, who suffered the just penalty of disobeying the Laws and the .Authorities. Let us, however, hope that we may never he called upon again, to chronicle such another event. Let us all, as good Citizens, be submis sive to the laws and our lawful superiors ! Let us, by our good conduct show, that we are worthy of enjoying the many privileges our illustrious Monarch is about to confer on us ! þÿ If this advice, as we hope it will, be carried into practice, we cannot but anticipate what we most sincerely wish our readers, A HAPPY NEW YEAR ! !

It has long been a wish, that divine

When one Danish church is open, the other is as yet generally shut up, although two ordained ministers of the Lutheran þÿ i. e. the dominant-church are residing in the respective towns of this island. In the latter time the whole work seems to have devolved on the one residing down here. We have frequently heard inquiries as to the cause of this anomaly, and whether it would ever be remedied. Here we have publicly repeated this grievance. Can and will Mr Verax, in our ignorance, tell us the truth? For it is perhaps rather presumptuous to expect such a condescension from those, who are best able to do it. No civilized person doubts the paramount importance of good schoolinstruction. We therefore leave to somebody, who may delight in rural excursions, to take a peep in the country-schools, and only take the liberty to ask, whether the public school in this town is actually satisfying every just claim, that can be made to a public school. From the scarcity of pupils latterly frequenting it, it would seem, that the Public does not think so. Is then the Public wrong? Or is the school

laboring under a consumptive disease, originating from a defective state of some component part of its organization? We suspect the latter to be the case. Does Mr. Verax think us right ? Therefore, if it be an error, that some people here are unprotected and oppressed, there exists, however, at this very time an impression in the minds of many of the inhabitants, that they belong to such a class, and this impression is nearly as bad as the reality. Nor can it be denied, since it is founded on fact, that people here, though often in distress bordering upon starvation, are not guarded and protected against swindling and rascality as, for instance, in England. There every swindler is immediately arraigned, of which the English papers contain numerous instances ; here your only chance is a private lawsuit, at which you must pay enormous charges for every witness that is heard, so you are, in reality, cut off in your design of gaining justice. þÿ Are we wrong in all this? What says Mr. Verax? A dreadful disease has now for some time made its ravages among us. Danish seamen from the brig of war, as well as Danish soldiers, have chiefly been its victims. They have certainly been brought in the public hospital in this town, and there attended to, no doubt, with as much care and skill as was ordinarily disposable; but we þÿ most of them have died. know that Extraordinary occasions demand extraordinary þÿefforts; but was this remembered and put into execution in the present case? Might not many valuable lives have been saved, if, in due time, the most scientific treatment, which a board of our best

medical men could suggest, had been duly applied? Such, at least, is the prevailing opinion, and we hope that Mr. Verax will not think it þÿ unwarþÿrantable, that we have propounded it here, since it is only done in order that, if we are wrong, we may gain a better information. If it should be thought, that our views in these important matters are not altogether erroneous, we would finally take the liberty to state, for mature consideration, what to us appears to be the primitive cause of all such defects in society as have here been pointed out. We are all, from nature, very fond of power and authority, except when it is used against ourselves. Therefore we poor mortals are always apt to rule our inferiors, if we are capable of doing so, even others, þÿ except they be of that interesting, tractable, obsequious kind, by whom a þÿman s s elf is readily, as it were, multiplied, þÿ but to indulge ourselves whenever and wherever it is practicable. But this self-indulgence creates a state of vapidness, so we do not easily overexert ourselves or weigh in our minds, what benefit our activity is to our fellow-beings ; considering ourselves as the centre of all creation we first ask : þÿ What good is that to me þÿ? T), hus gradually public life is petrified into a dead routine of mechanical form-service. This is a dreadful disease, as destructive to public life as yellow fever is to our terrestrial existence. Those, that have not from nature a healthful disposition, can

scarcely ever be cured from it. St Paul, however, has given a good receipt for it, when, in concluding his first letter to the Thessalonians, he says: þÿ Quench not the spirit." Frederiksted, December 24th 1852. The clerk of T. R. E.

To the Editor of the þÿ St. Croix þÿAvis. Sir! The term for which the members of the present Burgher Council have been appointed, will shortly expire ; consequently, a new election ought to take place.

The public, aware of the importance of reforms, which are in accordance with the interest of the community, has, ere this, adopted the preliminary steps, to meet the contingency, and to maintain, at the same time, their right ot appoint ing new members. It is currently reported, that in contradiction to that right, and owing to an unaccountable assumption, from what quarter, it is difficult to state, that this community, will be precluded that right, which it is its duty to protect, that the election alluded to, is not to take place, and that the present members, are to retain their situation independent of public suffrage, and in contradiction to public expectation. The inhabitants of St. Croix, have the privilege to elect annually, the members of their Burgher Council, and it would be preposterous, to imagine, that they would forego that right, þÿ why then, lower the degree of intelligence on the part of our community, as to suppose them insensible to the necessity of that organisation, which would give vitality to the Burgher Council, and thereby secure an independent representation. It is difficult to believe, that the members elected by the community, whose term of service are to expire, will boldly, in defiance to public opinion, retain their seats which is in direct violation of the principle to which they owe their present situation. Respect for the confidence of their constituents, demands another course, þÿ a course, dictated by prudence, if not by duty, and not to be

lost sight of by parties who are not altogether irresponsible, but, having accepted a public trust, renders their conduct open to comment. A few days will establish the correctness or otherwise, the rumours which are now in circulation, meanwhile, I hope this statement, will call that attention and vigilance, necessary, to guard the few and imperfect institutions which we can thus far boast of. A MEMBER. St. Thomas 15th December 1852.

THE GOLD DIGGING LOTTERY Some time ago a lad in the employment of Hcrapath's Railway Journal emigrated with his father and family to Australia, and, of course, repaired to the diggings. Altogether there were four, who dug seven holes without finding any of the metal which they sought. At the end of that time a solitary six-pence formed the united wealth. At length they dug an eighth hole, and were rewarded with 32 1. worth of gold. Continuing their labours, they had obtained, when the letter bringing the information left them, 141b. weight of gold þÿ about 6001b. in value. Such is the lottery of gold-hunting in the land said to be full of it. þÿ Hcrapath's Railway Journal.

There were present nt tho examination but 18 boys and girls ill the upper class. Needlework and embroidery form the only branch in which the children can he said to have learnt anything. The Lancosterian department is very good. The writer expresses his opinion that the teachers appear to have no method, and in the whole rates the school 2 degrees lower than ours. Whether the Burgher Council can consider for more advanced classes ? Surely j themselves justified in countenancing such a heavy outlay for such simple and imperfect education, is a question which we trust the members will settle consistently with the high responsibilities of their office. 1C 26th December 1852

i it furlheron leads to, that only satisfaction with their place ol residence, good will towards the owner or manager will keep the labourer on an estate, the public authority cat) hardly raise any objections against it. þÿ It can besides in regard to the fixed wages be observed, that whilst it here, just like in any other place where a great number of people are employed in doing the same wotk on the same spot is not feasible to pay to some wotkmen of the same class less than others, it is not accepted in practice, that the present regulations should be an obstacle to prevent work þÿ which requires more than ordinary skill or exertion, or is heavier than what a common 1st class labourer could execute, from being paid at a higher rate, a fact which does neither militate against the conception of the labouiers. That annual contracts are the rule, is with reference to the estates, based on practical circumstances: a year is the space of lime required to take off the crop and to establish the next one; the work is not interrupted by the seasons, and the extent of cultivation must in every way be regulated by the number of labourers on whose steady and continual i service can be calculated. The labourers themselves can have no reason for preferring another period; the most natural is, that the labourers, particularly those who have a family, should here as otherwhere, as long as they choose to work at all, be disinclined to change their abodes ; the best working people with families are inaccessible to the idea

ol being given warning; but precisely for the younger and more unsteady amongst them it is of importance that the duration of the contiacts should be stipulated thus that the chance of meditating and of practising such changing could not become too frequent. In as far as the legislative power has to follow a distinct principle and tendency in regulating these matters, it ought unquestionably to tie bent upon inducing the rural labouring population to remain settled in a certain place and to accustom themselves to regular work, and thus to prevent them from wandering about from one plaoo to another and thereby to acquire the habit of only working occasionally. When in these years many of them have left the sugar cultivation, it has only in very few instances been done with a clear prospect of attaining n more favourable position Experience has confirmed what was beforehand apprehended, viz , that the motive was a propensity to idleness and dislike of any kind of regular work. In how far the new law to prevent vagrancy will prove effective in checking and counteracting this propensity cannot be predicted. When the wish has been expressed that a class should form itself which corresponded willi the smaller farmers in Denmark, it must be remarked that our legislation does by no means prevent the division of the soil, and that there is no lack of ground, to be had at a reasonable price, but that the habits of the labourers arc in a great degree against the formation of such a class, at nnv rale for a

nearer future. The expenc.es connected with the erection ot separate buildirgs and their enclosures etc , are so considerable and the risk of seeing the work expended thereon lost by dint of the frequent spells of drought so striking, that no labourer who possesses a lew hundred of dollars could feel inclined to invest them in litis manner. In respect to day-labourers it is to be observed. that we know of no legal impediment to prevent nit individual, that has no other occupation, from seeking his maintenance in such a way ; hut still the ease never occurs that such a person should feel induced to seek day-labour in estates work ; a Inct which is particularly applicable to the many the unoccu- pied and unprovided inhabitants of towns. For him. who will seek work in the country, the advantages enjoyed by the legally engaged labourer are so proponderant that there can be no motive for rejecting such a position ; and as far as the employers ate regarded, who are however in no wise prohibited from renting out houses on their estates, none of them can be blind to that the admission on the estate of a person on account of the daylabour he was expected to execute would

excite the strongest dissatisfaction amongst the resident labourers, and, generally speakprecisely because a house and perquisites" ing lead to the removal of these " latter ones, on an estate are of such a significance, that such an occupant and eventual day-labourer would, beside an apparently much greater ges, personal independence, enjoy which for the attainment of all the advanta- the others would have to work the whole week Moreover the practical relations in regard to the real force of labour and the agricultural interest are of such a nature, that the formation of a class of day-labourers in the country must be looked upon as one of the greatest disasters which could possibly occur, be it to the country in general or especially to the rural population. As long as the legally engaged labourer is sought as he is now, and that will continue until either the number of them is augmented or the cultivation abandoned, it appeals palpable, that no class will appear which could be styled estate's-servanls, in as much as the difference would have to consist in the greater personal dependence of the latter. But if such so-called servants still were to enjoy the same privileges in respect to houses, limited hours of working, Saturday etc, wiih the resident labourers, they would merely be a class of common estate labourers, only engaged for a short time þÿ an institution by which the conditions for anything like stability, order and progress, which hitherto have prevailed in the country, would at once be

annihilated. We must be of opinion, that the rural relations in St. Thomas, on account of the vicinity of the large town and the unfavourable circumstances under which the estates labour, are of such a nature, which perhaps renders the legal rules, adapted to the other islands, less appropriate and that it generally speaking might be connected with great difficulties there to effect anything by legislation þÿ The Colonial Council can, just as little as the Government, propose any material alteration in the respective legal rules valid for this island. The Colonial Council has therefore arrived at the conviction, that it under existing circumstances must be advisable that no new and general law regarding the relations between estate owners and labourers in these islands should be issued. Whilst this is the primary report of the Colonial Council on this matter, we must at the same time for the ease, that it should not meet with yout Majesty's most gracious approbation, already at this early stage render our opinion on the law draft, laid before the Council. From Wilrner and Smith's European Times, January 2, 1853. THE NEW FRENCH CONSTITUTION

The following Senatus Consulturn is promulgated in the Moniteur, and has become fhe law of France. Napoleon, by fhe grace of God and the national will, Emperor of the French, to all present and to come, greeting: We have sanctioned and do hereby promulgate what follows: þÿ senatus consultum. Explaining and modifying the constitution of January 14, 1852. Art. 1. The Emperor has the right to grant pardons and accord amnesties. Art. 2, The Emperor presides, when he thinks proper, over the Senate and the Council of State. Art. 3: Treaties of commerce made in virtue of article 6 of the constitution

have the force of law for the modifications of the tariff therein stipulated. Art. 4. All works of public utility, and more especially those designated by article 10 of the law of the 21st April, 1852, and article 3 of the law of the 3nl May, 1841, and all enterprises of general interest, are ordered by decrees of the Emperor, Those decrees are issued in the forms prescribed by the regulations of the public administration. Nevertheless, if these works and undertakings have for condition, engagements, or money from the Treasury, the credit must be accorded, or the engagements ratified by a law, before the works are commenced. When the matter relates to works executed by the state, and which are not of a nature to become the object of concessions, the credits may he opened, in case of urgency, according to the forms prescibed for extraordinary credits. Such credits shall be laid hefore the legislative body at its next session. Art. 5. The dispositions of the organic, decree of the 22nd of March, 1852, may be modified by decrees of the Emperor. Art. 6. The members of the imperial family called eventually to the succession, and their descendants, are French princes. The eldest son of the Emperor takes the title of Prince Imperial. Art. 7. The French princes are members of the Senate and of the Council of State, when they shall have attained the full age of eighteen years. They can only take their seats by the consent of the Emperor. Art. 8. The acts of the etat civil of

the Imperial family are received by the Minister of State, and transmitted on an order of the Emperor to the Senate, which orders their inscription on the registers, and their deposit in the archives. Art. 9. The dotation of the crown and the civil list of the Emperor are regulated by a special Senatus Consultum. Art. 10. The number of senators nominated directly by the Emperor cannot exceed one hundred and fifty. Art. 11. An annual donation for life of thirty thousand francs is appropriated to the dignity of senator. Art. 12. The budget of expenses is presented to the legislative corps, with its administrative subdivisions, by chapters and Ity articles. It is voted by ministries. The distribution by chapters of the credit granted for each ministry is regulated by decree of the Emperor, pronounced in council of state. Special decrees, pronounced in the same form, can authorise transfers from one chapter to another. The disposition is applicable to the budget of the year 1853. Art. 13. The report of the debates ordered by Art. 42 of the constitution, is submitted, before its publication, to a commission, composed of the president of the legislative corps and of the president of each bureau. In case of an equal division of opinions, the president of the legislative corps shall have the casting vote. The proces verbal of the sitting read to the Assembly records merely the operations and the votes of the legislative corps. Art. 14. The deputies to the legislative corps receive an indemnity, which

is fixed at two thousand five hundred francs per month, during the continuance of each ordinary and extraordinary session. Art. 15. The general officers placed on the reserve may he members of the legislative body. They are to he considered as having given in their resignation, if they are employed in active service, in conformity with Art. 5 of the decree of Dec. 1, 1852, and with Art. 3 of the law of August 4, 1839.

Art. 16. The oath prescribed by Art. 14 of the Constitution is in the tollovving terms: "I swear obedience to the Constitution, and fidelity to the Emperor." Art. 17. Articles 2, 9, 11, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, and 37 (if the Constitution of the 14th January, 1852, are abrogated. Given at the Palace of the Senate, this 23rd of December, 1852. Mesnard, President. Baron T. df. Lacrosse, Cambaceres, Gen. Regnaud D'Angely, Secretaries. Examined and sealed with the seal of the senate, Baron T. de Lacrosse. We order that these presents, invested with the seal of the Senate, and inserted in the Bulletin des Lois, shall he addressed to the courts, tribunals, and administrative authorities, that they may inscibe them on their registers, duly observing the same and causing them to he observed; and our Secretary ofState for the department of Justice is charged to look to their pnblication. Given at the Palace of Compiegne, this 25th of December, 1852. Signed. Napoleon. Countersigned, Achille Fould, Minister of State. Examined, and sealed with the great seal, Abbaiucci, Minister of Justice.

The "AVIS." Christiansted , Tuesday the 8th February 1853. On Saturday last, a public meeting, as previously announced by the Secretary to the Board of Trustees of the St. Croix Savings Bank, was held in the Danish School-House; and was attended by His Excellency the Governor and Lady, together with a larue number of respectable Ladies and Gentlemen. We regret, however, to say, that but few of the labouring class were present. The Meeting was opened by the Secretary, J. H. Burt Esq , who, in a very lucid manner, gave many striking illustrations in proof of the usefulness of such an Institution. He then read, and commented on the Report of the Bank, dwel'ing, for some time, on the rapid progress ol the same, in the short space of eight months. He concluded by offering thanks to His Excelleney the Governor, for the many valuable favors which His Excellency has conferred on the Institution. The Rev. Mr. Endermami tlien addressed the Meeting, and regretted that that class of persons, viz: the labouring class, whom he would wish to have addressed, and whom lie expected to be present, were, unfortunately. absent. He regretted also that hut 1 1 of this elass of persons were depositors ; but endeavored to account for the fact, on the ground that very few of those persons could either read or write, and in their uneducated state could foim no idea of anything being theirs, which, they could not see and handle; consequently they could not consider that their money was as sale out of their sight, as when in their possession, lie proved very clearly that the object of such an In-

stitution, instead of b» ing as some suppose, contrary to the teachings of the Mcriptnres, was in fact support! d by many passages. He sincerely wished that the Institution may grow in strength, as it grows in years; and concluded by expressing his sincere thanks to His Excellency the Governor ; to the 1'resident, Treasurer, and other officers ol the SavingsBank, for the warm support they have rendered the Institution. The Reverend Mr Hawlev next addressed the Meeting, in a concise but very impressive manner, and stated that he felt himself called upon as a Minister of tho Gospel, to give his countenance to the Institution ; which he characterised as a higlier species of Chanty, than that ol Hospitals and Alms Houses, inasmuch as theae only took care of the I'oor and Destitute, while Savings Banks raised them to respect themselves and feel a manly dependence Ho doclared that tbo

s tr. « " ' ® © a a A'ns. ' progress of the Institution has surpassed his most sanguine expectations, and trusted that it would continue to progress and receive the kind support of his lellow Christians. The Meeting then closed.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis, Dear Sir ! I beg that you will allow me, through the medium of your columns, to call the attention of the authorities to a very novel instrument, which, it appears, has been introduced as a substitute for the G till) bee. On two occasions, in the course ofa mouth, the inhabitants dwelling in 1 lie vicinity of the House No. 11 Kings-Street in this town, have been altogether prevented from enjoying even the smallest portion of rest, being disturbed by the sounds of a bull-horn accompanied by a Violin and a Tambourine. The tones of this novel-instrument are even more annoying than the famed Gunibee; to which latter our ears had become somewhat accustomed, and which, although making a great noise, is not to lie compared to the former with its discordant and grating tones. I can scarcely doubt tint the Conch- Shell will next lie introduced as a bassinstrument to accompany this one. I must however consider, that, to allow such a barbarous instrument, þÿ the to les of which very closely resemble the bellowing of the animal which manufactures it, þÿ to be used in the centre of the town, is sanctioning as great a public nuisance as the Gumbee; against which, therefore, I beg leave to raise my voice. Yo ars, B.

Burt: " The author who informs us that his father is owner of an estate in St. Croix and that he, probably after having completed his education at Kiel and Copenhagen, was sent out to the colonies when the emancipation of the slaves had taken place in 1848 in order to take over the administration of the property, has made it his object to render clear to Danish readers how the events of the last years have affected the landed estates, their cultivation and the relations between labourers and employers, in as much an it cannot be indifferent whether garbled and silly or truthful and humane views prevail in the Diet, who will have considerable influence on tho regulation of the colonial affairs, whilst it as well can be to be clear, that there exists a want of appears surmised as, after what has been stated, knowledge of these affairs even with highly intelligent members of the Diet. The author must of course dwell upon the compensation question which forms the subject of frequent discussion in the colonies

and was brought in by government under the last session but did not come to an ultimate settlement, and has on account of the low amount proposed by no means met with undivided approval iu the colonies. The author urges strongly that this matter shoQld be brought to a speedy close, to the attainment of which object now also the Colonial Council of which he is a member, have done theirs by rendering a unanimously accepted report on the matter which in general leans towards the ministerial proposition, excepting however the amount and the position maintained that compensation is the fuifilm nt of a strictly legal claim. The author contributes in a very significant m inn :r to the elueid ition of the matter by publishing a series of documents from which it appears that Or ivjrnment up to a period shortly prooediag cinuieipitiiu has traded in slaves, that is to say, has sold slaves from one cstato to

n from the owners for sums which mortgage-bonds another and exacted payment or would exceed the proposed amount of compensation by three or four times and which the purchasers have been compelled to pay even long after emancipation. Such elucidations certainly deserve the attention of those who have an influence on or take an interest in these matters, for it will not do in any affair, may it nearly or distantly touch us, to turn a deaf ear to the voice of justice and public morals, and the State must rather bear a burden tban commit an act of injustice against a whole class of its burghers. The language of the author is not entirely free of German and English terms of phrases. The pamphlet has been distributed in the Diet and it must be hoped that the members of the same may have perused it." The benevolent inserter, whoever he be, has evidently and from good judgment postponed this advertisement until the day when the proceedings of the Diet were interrupted by the Christmas Holy Days, in order to engage the serious attention of the members at the precise moment when the hours of leisure were before them. We will hope that the joyous and elevated state of mind which is inseparable from Christmas may have rendered them more inclined to enter upon and investigate the clear and unquestionable claims of the colonies which are now submitted to their arbitration from a fair and just point of view. The debates on the compensation question were resumed the 6th January.

St. Thomas, West Indies. The Danish government has lately given a proof of its liberality and justice which is worthy of imitation hy other governments claiming to he Christian. The government has lately bestowed on its West India possessions a representative assembly, which is to meet annually at St. Croix, and the elections for w hich were held in all the islands on one and the same day. The governor, w hose seat ofgovernment is at St. Croix, possesses the power of fixing the day of election, and appointed Saturday, "the 28th of August last, for that purpose. This was announced in t lie papers on the 22nd of that month. Our respected co-religionist, Major Wolff, than whom no man in the island of St. Thomas is more esteemed, thereupon wrote to a Christian friend at St. Croix, requesting him to call on his exellency, ami to state that he (Major W ) was sure that the governor must have forgotten that the day appointed for the elections was the Jewish Sabbath, and that, in consequence, many Jews would he prevented from voting; and that as Major Wolff had been appointed one of the judges of the poll, he would also have to decline. With that justice and liberality which lias uniformly actuated our highly-esteemed governor, he at once acknowledged the propriety of the appeal, and altered the day of election to Monday the 30th of August. This fact is honourable, not only to the governor, hut 1o our brethren, on whose behalf the day of election was altered. Ii shows, also, what may he done if Jews do Imt
take the opportunity of making their complaints known in the proper quarter. þÿ The Jewish Chronicle, London, Jan. 1 4th 1853.

The above result of the operation of the Savings Bank in the first seven months of its existence is no doubt highly satisfactory both with regard to the number of individuals, who have availed themselves of this institution, and to the amount of deposits and the inconsiderable amounts which in proportion have been withdrawn from the Bank. But if it, on the other hand, be taken into consideration that one of the chief objects of the institution has been to procure 1'or the laboring population of the country a proper place for depositing their savings, in safety from thefts or from the temptation of being squandered, it is certainly a matter of surprise, that so very few of this class have shown any inclination of availing themselves of the institution, but this may be accounted for by observing that

whilst the population of the towns, from its manifold connections with the Island of St. Thomas, has already for several years been acquainted with or at all events heard of the utility of the Bank of that place, the whole institution is still new to the country population. When it shall have existed for some years and gained more and more the confidence of the one class of the population, it may be reasonably expected that the other will follow.
