In compliance with the request contained in our last number, we have procured the manuscript of the address, with which the Secretary of the Savings Bank Jou\ II. Buut Esq. gies, who and opened the public meeting en Saturday " Inst. It runs as follows: Ladies nnd Gentlemen ! It must naturally be a very difficult and arduous undeitaking to condense all that can be said, and that has been said, in praise and commendation of an in titution like the Savings Banks, within the narrow limits of a short speech, or some introductory remarks to the Report on the actual financial state of our own Bank, and the results attained during the brief space of its existence, which is now to be imparted to you. I, at any rate, feel myself embarrassed, it not overpowered, by the inexhaustible richness ot the subject : still I deem it highly desirable that the salutary consequences and beneficial effects that spring from an institution which, since the end of the last centurv, has more and more spread the blessings i shallow pleasure, connected with wise foresight, noble industry and persevering diligence, over bling. numberless communities of England, Scotland, France and Germany, should once more in their impressive simplicity nnd imposing truth lie laid before this honoured assembly; this must be the more desirable as we as yet have only to do with a feeble beginning. The future success of our Bank can not be foretold, it is still to be guaranteed and effected, and we must base all our ex-

fident hope of the strenuous upon pectation ol such success co-operation the conarid unswerving interest to be evinced 1 y all classes ol the community. Nobody should stand aloof and remain indifferent, for, nobody can be said to find himself in so utterly isolated a position, that he should want the opportunity of

3'JS © & at X ATI'S exercising a beneficial influence in furthering our object. The good word, the kind and well-meant advice, go a great way when properly uttered and impressively tendered. It is certainly not an exaggeration when Michel Chevalier, whilst investigating the causes of the misery prevailing establish a system of " organisation of among be working classes, and trying to labour" that could remedy them, maintains : "The Savings B inks are deserving of all care and protection on the part of any public authority which has at heart to elevate and improve the tn iterinl and moral condition of the worthing classes. Their utility is not confined to the laying-by of means in the days of prosperity for the evil days to come, and thus to cause the labourer to contribute to the formation of capital, this wielder of the magic wand of which he has to expect so much. The Savings Banks have a most remarkable effect upon the morality of men. As soon as At the request of Christiansteds Deal- ! lie becomes a depositor, the labourer

From this moment be knows what foresight is. The future gains in his eyes a significance, life an object. "-r-Nor can Charles Du/hii be said to go too far, when lie in his very popular little work "on Savings Banks" exclaims; "lioiv iii iny hidden virtues, bow much self-control, bow much resistance to the seductions of pleasure and the allurements of debaucht rv, bow much filial and parental love, how many providential inspirations and religious sentiments are laid down and concealed in the capital of a Savings Bank, hoarded up cent hy cent and collected by the sweat of the brow of the labouring classes!" þÿ And certainly the simple but striking words which have been inserted in « lie fly-Tcaf of our deposit-books deserve the serious notice of every labourer who is not yet a depositor ! þÿ Thus I could go on for a while recapitulating the sentiments of the wisest and best men, precisely those who have sacrificed their time dedicated their best enerhave themselves watched the practical effects of this institution with intenseanxiety ; but 1 will rather, for the sake of briefness and lucidity, try to point out in some concise sentences the unquestionable fruits which the Savings Banks have borne in Europe. Firstly. They have tended to preserve anil augment capital in a country. Secondly, They enable the labourer to render bis earnings and hoardings productive at once, whilst it would have been difficult for him to find an investment without the existence of a Savings

Baitk. Thirdly. The facility of instant investment shields him front the temptation of spending bis money in frivolous pursuits or debauchery. Every small amount which is deposited in the Bank would but too easily be squandered in or by indulging in injurious habits, such as drinking or gam-

Fourthly. The Savings Banks afford an outward safety, þÿ mean against theft þÿ which is wanting in private houses Fifthly. They tend to keep the unexperienced and confiding labourer out of the reach of designing swindlers. Sixthly and lastly. From a more general point of view, as indicated above, they guarantee to him a reserve fund to fall back upon in cases of sickness and wanting labour, and must thus have the effect of securing to him an independence that, cannot fail to strengthen a manly and dignified confidence in himself and his own powers, lie knows that he, if providence visits him or his with disasters, has the means of militating against, of mending them by the results

of bis own previous foresight, that he like a man can stand on bis own legs and provide for himself and li is family, and is raised beyond the humiliating necessity of begging or of applying for public relief from poor-funds etc. I shall now turn to the more individual and practical task, which lias assembled us here and read up the Report of the Board of Trustees. ( Vide Front Faze.) When we examine the list more minutely according to the personal station and occupation ot the depositors, it must at once strike us that people of all classes in the towns have entrusted to us their savings. W e sec w ith delight that wise parents have regularly sent their children with small amounts, the results, we suppose of kind presents given to them at an early age with the distinct view of imbibing them in time with the habits of order and economy . It must gratify us in the highest degree to receive so signal a mark of confidence in the institution as is clearly evinced by the deposits effected by guardians for minors; they evidently understood its value and knew how to appreciate the opportunity offered them of a safeinimediateand intermediate investment. The considerable and regular deposits of our soldiers are highly commendable, nor are we ignorant of, or ungrateful for, the strenuous exertions made by their commanders in order to convince llieni of the safety and utility of the Bank. We also know of many employers who have been equally zealous in persuading their servants to bring us the part of their

wages for which they had no immediate use. Of the great body of country-labourers we have only to announce, as depositors þÿ 11. Not as if this very scanty proportion could in hi y way lie a matter of astonishment to us. It was clearly foreseen and repeatedly foretold, that a longer space of tune must elapse before they would gain confidence in such an institution, and arrive at t lint height of self-denegation which unquestionable is requisite for the labourer w ho is expected for the first time to make tip his mind to renounce the immediate use and disposition of bis money. Still I see no class in this community upon which the moral support and the exercise of selfcontrol w hich are offered and rendered easy here, would tell better, was it only on account of their childish inexperience and foolish manner of putting up their money. How often have not we people of the country to listen to grievous complaints of money being stolen out of negro-houses that was hidden beneath the floor, in a crevice of the wall, in an old pot or under some dirty rags! But the difficulty of inducing them to entrust their boardings to the Savings Bank lies, as far as the industrious and Irnrd-working amongst them arc concerned, in a general undefined and vague distrust. Money which they can not at any time sec and handle appears to them as unsafe, as half lost from the moment tliey part with it ; they can not be brought to comprehend and receive the notion of a tangible security and guarantee. Let every bedy do bis

best to convince them that those who have voluntarily charged themselves with the direction of this Bank do not earn gain and profit, but risk and responsibility, loss of time ! It is moreover obvious, not pleasure, but labour and that in many instances the dark hints and unconscientious insinuations thrown out by people w ho would blacken and counteract any beneficial pub/ic undertaking in order to promote their own selfish and undermining purposes are applied to deter the industrious labourer. In this respect I will beg leave to quote

the answer which was given to a friend of mine who tried to induce one of his best-disposed workmen to deposit Ins money in the Savings Bank. The man had accumulated a considerable sum of money and was almost willing to yield to the persuasive proposition of his employer, if oidy from personal regard and confidence; but a'l at once suspicion ami and he said : distrust got the upperhand in his mind " But, Massa, supposing there was a crash !" þÿ The expression itself seems to show that the idea had been put into his head by somebody who certainly took good care not to explain to him that the effects of such a "crash" could not possibly ever reach and affect him and his money ! þÿ n regard to the rest, the far greater portion of the country labourers, the difficulty lies, as far as the females are concerned in their propensity for frippery, showy dresses and many other kinds of foolish expenditure. 1 could not help looking at the silver dollars suspended on the necks and attached to the rose-coloured dresses of the queens and their maids of honour in the last Christinas processions, without indulging in a sigh and in the sincere regret that we had not those dollars and the amount of the costs of those tawdry and tasteless dresses in the coffers of our Bank. As for the men þÿ and this is a very serious and melancholy point þÿ the stumbling block is to he found in their vicious habits, in the dice arid the ruin-bottle þÿ two fearful enemies to anything like future civilization, which

grow in strength day for day. Though I could, from my own individual experience, quote sundry awful examples of negroes breaking their necks in the excess of intoxication, of others that struck me with horror by the frantic ravings of delirious maniacs, I will not dwell upon so distressing a subject any longer. Enough of it ; let us hope to God that when we meet again next year we may be able to lay before this honoured assembly a more cheering report of the ! numbers of deposits from the country I will rather turn to subjects of a pleasant nature ; I mean the kind assistance with which we have met from so many 6ides. The number of subscribers is large enough for so small a community, to be considered at once as a clear proof of a general and lively interest in the undertaking; it has at all events sufficed to secure a fair start and good beginning. And certainly the progress has been attended with the most welcome encouragement and meritorious liberality from sundry quarters. Whilst the first idea of establishing a Savings Bank in St. Croix emanated from His Excellency the Governor, we must moreover express the sense of our obligation for the readiness with which he, to promote the beginning of the institution, placed the necessary locality at our disposal in Government House. The same assistance was tendered by Mr. F. A. Luntl, who, with equal liberality, granted the use of his office to the Branch Bank at West End, where Mr. J. N. Schou has hitherto with

the most praiseworthy disinterestedness gratuitously performed the functions of an Accountant. We have moreover gratefully to acknowledge the generosity with which the Directors of the St. Thomas Bank have allowed interest on any amount, which we at any time might deposit in the hands of their Agency. We have undoubtedly Major KeutsJi and his kind intercession to thank for such a favour; however he did not subsist here, hut has also taken upon himself the office of Treasurer and the neatly kept books will ever form a lasting monument of his merits in furthering the youthful institution. Thus nothing is now remaining hut that the Board of Trustees, impressed

<0 IB þÿ ¬> S with lively gratitude for all the aid and assistance with which they have hitherto been favoured, should once more urge the future of the Savings-Bank upon the serious attention of the public at large, without which they, as stated above, can not entertain any hope of its success"

The þÿ AVIS. Christiansted, Tuesday the 15 th February 1853. The Compensation Kill. We have the gratification of again announcing to our readers, that this bill was on the 5th ult. re-introduced in the Folkething by the Minister of Finance, Count Sponneck, and of laying before the public a translation of the þÿMinister speech s on the occasion. While we feel ourselves bound to declare, that we are much beholden to the noble Count for bringing forth the matter at such an early period, considering the time when the report of the Colonial Council was received by the Home Government, we cannot avoid deprecating the discrepancy between the amount proposed by the Minister, namely $50 per head and that demanded by the Colonial Assembly, $75 for each slave. We find this discrepancy the more astonishing as the Miuister himself admits, that the Assembly rest satisfied in demanding less than the value of the slaves. Nor are we less grieved at perceiving, that the Minister yet persists in denying the claim to compensation to be founded on strict law. So much has been written and so much has been said about the question, whether the claim of the late slave owners to compensation is legal or not, that we would cheerfully refrain from arguing the point further, wore we not constrained to do so from an observation of the Minister, which appears, contrary to his view of the matter, conclusive, that the slave owners have a legal right to compensation. The Minister states, and justly too, that the Mortgage-holders in the late slaves have an unrestricted right to the compensation

which will be granted for the slaves mortgaged. Now it is evident, that if the mortgageholders had a legal right in the slaves mortgaged, the owners must likewise have had a legal right in the slaves : for it follows as a natural consequence, that the owners could not lawfully mortgage what they had no legal right to. Or, if the compensation be granted as an act of charity, the mortgageholders cannot have a better right to the compensation sum than other creditors of the recipient of the donation. But, as it is incontrovertible, that the mortgageholders have a legal right to the compensation sum, it is likewise incontrovertible, that the late slave owners have a legal right to compensation. This view of the matter no doubt led the Colonial Council to reject the proposed restrictions in the right of the mortgageholders ; for while they maintained that the right of the late slave owners is sacred they could not with any shadow of justice admit of any restrictions in a right equally inviolable. Without being very sanguine, we arc pemtaded that as the Minister is now gone a step further in proposing $50 per head in compensation, the Diet, in consideration that even $75 for each slave is not adequate, will yet go a step further in granting the sum proposed by the Colonial Council.

SPEECH OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE. It will be remembered, that in the last session of the Diet a Bill on the same subject was brought forward as the present one, which according to His þÿMajesty commands s I now have the honor of laying before the House. That bill did not progress through the various stages ; and as the Colonial Council, whioh in the meanwhile has been established, has been occupied in discussing tho matter, I have not been able at an earlier period to re-introduce the subject. Tho report of tho Colonial Council was rcoeived at the close of lost year ; in the report, which will bo laid before the Honorable Houso as a voucher to the bill, every attention possible has been paid to the wishes expressed in the Colonies in regard to the whole detail and form of tho bill, under which the compensation that may be granted, ought to be given to tho parties concornod. I would call to mind, that tho Government in introducing tho former bill in tho last session maintained, that the lato slave owners in the danish westindia possessions

8 sn XL A T had no legal light to compensation for the value þÿ which the unfree had, before they were emancipated ; it was however urged by the Government, that they bad a claim founded on common justice and equity, which, although not of tbe same nature, was yet similar to those, wbicL on many former occasions bad been admitted, and in a liberal manner liquidated here in Dcnmaik, and chiefly by the concurrence of the Diet. It was therefore to be expected, likewise in consequence of the petitions, which during earlier sessions had been received by the Diet from the Wcstindies, that the Colonial Council would not take the same view of the subject as the Government. The Honorable House will find in the report of the Colonial Council, that they have positively maintained, that the other (?) slave owners had a legal right ; but in demanding the settlement of their lawful claims, they have not arrived at the conclusion of insisting on the payment of the full value ; they are satisfied with less. I have naturally, in regard to this part of the report of the Colonial Council, found myself bound to give the matter the most serious consideration ; but Ilis þÿMajesty s Government have not been able to arrive at any other conclusion, in respect to the legal nature of the claim in question, than the one already stated, and in as far as concerns the principal point of the matter, they cannot recommend the demand of the Colonial Council. His þÿMajesty s Government have, however, concluded, that þÿ partly with

regard to the present better prospects ol the financial resources of the Monarchy ; which now present themselves, in comparison with the prospects at the time when the question was first mooted, and partly as a year is lost, during which, those for whom the compensation is now demanded have lost the interest of the amount, þÿ there were sufficient grounds, under the observance of the same principle, that no legal right could be admitted, but a claim founded on common justice and equity) 1 g>vc tbe certainly hard pressed former possessors of slaves a greater amount of compensation than that at first proposed. The Governþÿment proposal s in the former session advocated, that the compensation should be based on an average of 40 westindia dollars per head ; in lieu of this it is proposed in the draft which I now have the honor of presenting to grant 50 westindia dollars, with the modification, however, in the following paragraphs of the Bill, that the interest of the bonds, with which the claims is to be chiefly covered, will commence a year later than stipulated in the former draft. I must in this respect beg to remark, that this question of interest is not confined merely to that which is recommended in the present Bill, namely 4 per cent, but it extends to a more considerable amount, in as much as a greater scarcity of money in the Westindies has occasioned, that the ordinary rate of interest cannot be considered to be there 6 per cent, as it was the case formerly under more favorable circum-

stances ; but it has in these pressing years risen to 9 a 10 pr. ct., it is consequently a much greater loss, which the delay of the matter represents for the respective individuals, for whom compensation is demanded than the simple interest of tho bonds. It is with these views, but always on tho same basis, on which the original draft was founded, that I have the honor of appearing with tho present hill. With regard to the respective paragraphs, it is very satisfactory to me to be able to recommend, that in this respect the proposals of the Coloniul Council should be entirely adopted, and it is a greater source of gratification to me to be able in this case to state, that these proposals are in harmony with my conviction, as it is the first question, which, after having been treated in the Westindia Colonial Council, now is to be discussed in the Danish Legislature. There i6 one point only, which may give rise to some doubts, and that is the position of the creditors, namely those who held mortgage in the lofmcr slaves. In the draft, laid before the House in the fmmer session, there were some restrictions intended in the rights of mortgageholders, as it was deemed desirable, in imitation of instances in foreign countries, as much as possible to secure the non-perversion of the compensation sum. But the Colonial Council have decided against such restrictions ; and on that account only I would find sufproposal ; but ficient grounds for deviating from the original I likewise find rt the less necessary,

as the motives which led other States to make such restrictions as proposed in the first draft are less apparent at a period when the emancipation for years had already taken place, as is the case with our Islands, than when the compensation is granted immediately ; for it is self evident, that, when compensation is immediately granted, there is a greater probability, that the compensation sum, in lieu of being applied to tho cultivation of tho estates, will be remitted to foreign countries, and thus not bo appropriated to tho benefit of those parts of the State, which the Legislature

3 thereby intended to assist. This fear is naturally of less extent, when the emancipation has already taken place for several years, which of necessity has occasioned, that means have already been procured by the same men, to whom the compensation sum will be paid, and have been appropriated to the improvement of the cultivation. þÿ - v <.<- The Dominican Schooner of War Constitucion, Captain Ramon Solis, arrived here yesterday from St. Domingo, having on board Messrs. T£1E REV. H. W. REECHEES. Wc deem no apology necessary for introducing the subjoined anecdote into our columns. It will be read with interest by those who admire boldness in the cause of truth ; and wc may add, that we present it on the authority of a gentleman who was present when the incident occurred. The ltev. 11. W. Beecher is a brother of Mrs. þÿStowe s and pastor of an Independent congregation at New Yoik, which includes a considerable number of individuals professing pro-slavery views. Departing from the ordinary rule of the American pulpit, with reference to the question of slavery, Mr. Beecher has courageously and pertinaciously denounced the institution and its advocates, though at the risk of losing some of his wealthiest supporters. Shortly after the passing of the Fugitive Slave Law, his congregation subscribed a sum of money for the puiposc of presenting him with a testimonial, which ultimately assumed the shape of a handsome carriage. Amongst the contributors were many of those whose views on the slavery question were diametrically opposed to his own. On the Sunday subsequent to the presentation of this mark of respect, and whilst acknowledging it in suitable terms, he turned towards a particular section of his flock, and pointedly addressing þÿ them, said : þÿ And now that you have been kind enough to give me a carriage, 1 will tell you what I intend to do with it. The very first slave that is making his escape from slavery, and asks me to help him off,
shall have a seat in that carriage ; and if there is no one else to drive him into Canada, I will get on the box and take the reins myself. þÿ þÿ St. Christopher's Gazette.

As the superior authority is the one unto whom the Policemaster (according to the draft publication paragraph 1 in fine) would have to apply in doubtful or important cases and whose instructions or orders they (agreeably to the same) would have to obey, and whereas the question relative to the limits of the superior authoiity here cannot be brought ; merly was carried on by the Royal Council, before the tribunals, so as in the mother country, according to the fundamental law, there will be no other remedy against the arbitrary proceedings or mistakes of the Police Magistrates, than complaint to the Ministry or to His Majesty, which in the daily Police-suits, that takeu by themselves may be less significant, but in their union very important, might be tantamount with a total denial of justice. We cannot therefore find the proposed change of the judicial and Police department to be by far either suitable or safe. To join the posts of Judge Advocates for the Garrisons with such inferior offices as the proposed Policemasters, is no guarantee for the safety of the proceedings of the Military Courts of Justice, which particularly in distant colonies seem to require more cate. With respect to the proposed chief Authority for St. Thomas, we think it our duty to state that it is a generally acknowledged truth, which even the present Minister of Finance has applied to the existing chief Authority in St. Thomas, þÿ that in the West-

indies have been created grand titles and relations for small þÿobjects þÿ vide Proceedings of the Diet (Landsthing 1852) No. 94. Although it has now been proposed to modify this somehow, by limiting the chief Authority to that of a President ; we are of opinion, that a further step may be taken in the reduction of expences by doiny away entirely with this chief Magistrate for a territory which scarcely can be viewed otherwise than a larger town or country jurisdiction n Denmark. As far as it has been intended, that the President should take over the military command. we avail ourselves of this opportunity to express our opinion' that the existing combination of civil and military functions ought as soon as possible to cease, and the Military, with respect to the detail, be put under an entirely independent Authority, who, as well as the chief in command in every garrison, only would have to give assistance when called upon. On this footing the Military in the English Islands are pul to the Governor, even if he be a military man. In our islands there would be so much more cause to follow the same principle, as there are weighty reasons, why the Governor ought þÿ not as is the case in the French islands a military character þÿ to be a jurist, who being a civil functionary cannot generally be expected to be possessed of the requisite knowledge and sense of military affairs, so that, while the military details take up his time to the detriment of other much more important business, his ignorance

of military details may easily so much disturb the acting of the whole military machine, that its strength and activity would be wasted. The means of having a military commander in chief separated from the civil administration, has also been pointed out in the military plan of 5th May 1851, which makes the eldest officer the Commander of the Military with addition to his salary as chief in command, and when you make over to him the necessary aid in the military Aid de-camp and the military clerk, who now are both used by the Governor, he will easily be able to get through the business. With respect to the civil affairs of the suserve ; without entering here into an ex- perior þÿ authority at St Thomas we will obtensively detailed representation thereof; þÿ court might be held that, after having carefully examined their nature, we have arrived at the result, that without any difficulty and even without any considerable addition of business for the Gov-

8 m © a s: A?n, ernor in St Croix, they can be made over to him, which would be both the cheapest and the only means to secure to St. Thomas the same legal condition as St. Croix, particularly at a time, when you wish to put in force new and very important laws, which otherwise very easily might be made an object of different interpretations by different authorities. When we say that such a change would, in our opinion not increase the business very much for the Governor in St. Croix, we believe that the most important part of the business of the Chief Magistracy, that for-

were already during Councellor þÿHansfn s Government transferred over to St. Croix, and that at least some business, which is here transacted by the Chief Magistracy, are in Denmark transacted by the subordinate authorities, for instance the very frequent appointments of Guardians, which in Denmark are issued by the Magistrates, where such are, and otherwise by the Dealing- Master in the country in Tiis capacity of Upper Guardian. A parcel of expeditions respecting assignments for money may no doubt be simplified; thus the many monthly assignments for salary might be avoided by one stand ing assignment, to be valid until countermanded, which we believe is the case in the country-treasuries in Denmark. That the chief magistrate will be exempted from a great deal of details by a regulation of the communal concerns is likewise evident. The þÿ AVIS. Christiansted, Friday , thc2oth February 1853. The following is translated from þÿ Bigsdagslidtnde" No. 155: þÿ SPEECH of the Hon. Lehmann on the Compensation-Bill. þÿ The honorable Minister of Finance has, in laying before the House the pvosent Law-Draft, reminded the same, that it was the first subject which, after having been laid before the established Colonial Council in the Westindies, came over to the Diet for discussion. This is a consideration which I, under general circumstances, would be inclined to attach groat weight ; but I think, that every person will make the allowance, which I at least must make on my part, that 1 have both very little knowledge of and not so much energetic interest for these distant Islands, which formerly, at least the largest of them, directly was purchased, and is essentially cultivated by a negro population, who is not entirely in common with us Danes, and for a greater part has been owned by strangers. Therefore will I be inclined to grant the Colonial Council, in the management of the internal affairs of the Islands, a liberty and power, which yet goes further than the Law- Draft, wodn its time have discussed, and therefore will I always be inclined, with regard to the order of their own internal affairs, to add to their wishes and views of the matter an extraordinary great influence ; but I yet believe, that this regard can not have the same meaning, where it concerns a question, not as to how their own in-

ternal affairs there should be managed ; but where it concerns our money here. In this case I believe, that the Colonial Council, although it surely is a legal and an acknowledged representative body for the Islands, yet in a point of view regarding petitions it stands only as deliberative, in respect to the Mother Country ; wherefore it appears to me that the elucidations that present themselves here, with regard to the loss the Islands must have sustained by emancipation and the like, have equality only next to those petitions we have received from paper-manufacturers, sugar-refiners and the like, wherein they state the reasons which express their wishes, and which can only be considered as advice to the executive power here. 1 have been obliged to premise this consideration, because 1 Mippnse that we, in this case, perhaps, will come to lay lesser weight on their wishes in the course of time than we in all those eases, that concern the management of their own internal affairs, certainly will be inclined to do, as often as a Law-Draft with their report thereon is laid before us. I shall for this reason, and for the present, not dwell much on those considerations advanced by the Colonial Council ; but only remark, that if the matter is looked upon in the same point of view as that taken by the Colonial Council, it would have been wiser if it had laid less weight on the severe and bare idea of property ; for if it were true that the slaves, when the final emancipation took place, were in reality

a pure and clear property, then I believe þÿ and this is something we need not suppress þÿ that it will not he denied, that real slaves which are considered and treated as property, arc bound in no way by laws which are given with regard to property j but are perfectly entitled to throw off that- yoke, standing only under the right of the stronger one, which yoke does not becomes than until the oppressed himself last longer þÿ the stronger one. 1 believe in the mean time it and I have already taken the liberty to express þÿ that the emancipation was already so prepared during a very long series of years, that it is only highly improper that we should consider the la-

boring population, which stood under such conditions as at that time really existed in the Westindies, as a simple object of property, and that it is positively inconsistent with the pure, dry. idea of property, that the slaves themselves could have property and could purchase themselves and the like. I beli ve that the emancipation took place in reality in 1847, from that moment no slave could any longer be born in the Islands, and that the teim which was lixed until this work of freedom should be introduced perfectly, is properly nearest to be compared together, it has likewise without a doubt received its model in the same respect as it was introduced by the English emancipation act, just as well also is it clear to every one, that that term of apprenticeship was shortened without any great difficulty, aud without being properly considered a step of peculiar decisive importance, in as much as it is well known, that it was in the like manner grounded on the þÿplanters as w< 11 as on the þÿnegroes interests, as it was evident from all sides, that it was impossible to keep a population in a kiud of slave condition, after their liberty was expressed, after there already was an unquiet, a burning longing for liberty with this people, just as well as it was evident, that it was impossible to get free laborers to woii; together with people, that yet stood in such a relation to slavery. I believe also, that the final emancipation had gone before, and that its sudden and complete introduction in

every respect was called forth by occurrences, which Denmark and the Danish Government could not be made answerable ; lor it is clear, that we shortly after could have disavowed it, but I believe, and certainly every person must agree with me in th i-, that, after liberty was placed in view by the Danish Government, particularly during a time when Europe and all the colonies were in a state of commotion, it would have been impossible to bring the negroes back to any state of thraldom. It is with these few remarks I will express my preliminary opinion, that it is in every respect only equitable that something be granted here, and that it is a question, which demands an earnest consideration, if it can be maintained, to burden the danish taxpayers with such a compensation, in any ease to a certain extent, and I mean likewise, that it must be a matter, that deserves earnest consideration, if any difference could be made between the town and country negroes, in as much as it is my perfect and entire conviction, that with more and greater right is it evident, that the condition of the negroes was good already before the emancipation, and the more must it be acknowledged, that they must have had it about the same as the labouring population now lias it and which is the only tiling the entire large mass of the laboring population anywhere attains. I believe also, that this subject in some respect, can serve as a model for that importance which we in other matters will ascribe to the Colonial Council, and
that the present Law Draft dc serves an earnest consideration ; wherefore I shall also, in due time, move that it be banded over to a committee for discussion.

Christiansted, St. Croix 17th January 1853. DIED early on Saturday morning the 15th instant, George Lawrance Esquire, commanding Her Britannic þÿMajesty Surveying s Ship Scorpion, and whose funeral took place the same evening, accompanied with every mark of military honor, which could be shown by this Government, and the deepest sympathy, on the part of every respectable inhabitant of this place, who attended the solemn and mournful procession. The death of Lieutenant Lawrance is a public loss, not alone to his Nation, but to the service of Navigation in general. For some years past, he has been employed in surveying the Virgin Islands, including Crab Island and Culebra, with all their Reefs and Passages, and which having lately completed, he came to this Island to survey its Coast and Reefs also. In this occupation, which occasionally exposed him to great fatigue, his valuable life was closed at the early age of 36 years, deeply lamented by the few surviving officers of the Scorpion, and every other person who had the honor of his acquaintance. His skill and talents as a Surveyor, are conspicuous, in those charts of the British Virgin Islands which are already published, and equally so in his surveys of the Danish Islands, St. Johns, St. Thomas, and the numerous small Islands and Channels connected with them, which were shown to the writer by Lieutenant Lawrance himself, and which when published, accompanied with the numerous beautiful views Na- he has taken, will leave nothing further for the

vigator to desire ; but his Surveys were not confined to these Islands, for his field of action has extended over the West Indies generally, the Bahamas, the Gulph of Mexico and other places, so that grief and regret become tlio more acute, that a life so honorably and usefully employed, should have so suddenly terminated. He leaves a wife and young family in Bermuda, to deplore his irreparable loss A L

To Mr. B. If really you are in earnest with your advising me to decline further controversy with you, your last article cannot but serve the purpose admirably, it being in fact so peculiar an example of penmanship, that it safely can be left to its fate. To add to superfluity, however, you first declare, that there has been no occasion for my meddling with your criticism, and afterwards recommend your advice by terming the controversy needless. What then? A criticism, set down by its author as neither occasioning nor needing any reputation, can doubtless also by the party assaulted be treated with indifference. Now you certainly have the right to rate your own arlicles as low as ever you please ; but, although, in consequence of your own appraisement of what you hitherto have produced, I can, for the future, humour you by disregarding anything you may think proper to advance, still 1 cannot give you credit for good-will either towards the school or the teachers. Yours very respectfully, ' C. N. LUND, Teacher in the Danish school. 20th January 1853.

We copy from the þÿ New York þÿHerald, of the 7th Jany., the following very interesting account of the successful trial trip, on the 4th instant, of the Caloric Ship Ericsson : In the great commercial and shipping circles of the world, nothing has exited more interest of late than the novel discovery and enterprise of Capt. Eiiesson, by which steam as a motive power is to be supplanted by calorie or heated air ; and nothing hut the successful application of the actual test could remove the skepticism with which generally the project has been viewed. This test has, however, at length been furnished, and now all doubts of the practicability and importance of the invention are dispelled. The ship Ericsson, constructed on the new principle, made her trial trip on Tuesday morning down the hay of New York, and from the complete triumph with which the experiment was attt nded, there need now be no hesitation in acknowledging calorie as a great natural element adapted to locomotion destined to work a complete revolution in navigation and to confer an inestimable benefit on mankind. The Ericsson was put under caloric early on Tuesday morning and started from Williamsburg between nine and ten þÿo clock. At 9 h. 56 m., , at 10 h. 30 in. and 30 seconds, she was abreast she passed the flag staff on þÿGovernor Island, s and Fort Diamond thus mating a distance, of seven and three-eights miles in thirty four minutes and thirty seconds. From thence she proceeded down the bay, rounded to below Spit Head buoy at 1 1 h.

21 m. and there anchored in consequence of a snow squall. She returned on Wednesday, and anchored off the Battery at about, two þÿo clock in the afternoon. The distance between the stated points on þÿGovernor sIsland and Fort Diamond, being accurately known by triangulation to he seven miles, 660 yards, the speed attained was as stated about fourteen miles an hour. The consumption of fuel is ascertained to be only six English tons per twenty four hours , a sift ing, as

compared with steanships of more than eighty per cent. As the ship draws 16 feet 10 inches on an even keel this performance at a first trial, has astonished all concerned in the enterprise. The great idea which had for more than twenty years been ripening in the brain of the inventor, but which from trie incredulity and opposition he encountered among men of capital in Iris own native country, in England and in America, he had been unable to realize, lias thus been substantiated as a real entity. It was fortunate for Captain Ericsson and for the world, that one of our own enterprising merchants, John B. Kitching, Esq., who appreciated and relied on his talent and genius, determined at all risks to enable him to make the experiment on a scale worthy of the magnitude of the issue. For this purpose t lie latter furnished half of the capital necessary for the enterprise, and disposed among his acquaintances of the remainder of the stock, By this means, and regardless of expense the clipper ship whose first performance we have recorded, was built at the yard of Perrine. Patterson &. Stack and fitted up with enginery on the caloric principle under the immediate direction and supervision of Capt. Ericsson. The vessel measures of 260 feet in depth of hold is 27 of feet, Like the Arabia, length of deck, and 40 feet in her breadth the Cunard line, she has hut two and burthen 2,200 tons. beam; her masts, and like our swiftest clippers, she is extremely sharp in the prow. She of has two stern presents the device no figure head. Her figures, allegorical

representation of the United States and Great Britain placing a wreath around the brow of the inventor. She had been originally named the Caloric, hut in compliment to the genius who planned her, her name was changed to the Ericsson. This was considered by Captain Ericsson a high tribute to himself, but the flattering device which was placed upon the stern without his knowledge, overwhelmed him with emotion, and wo arc told that when he first saw it, he wept like a child. The Ericsson presents a very handsome and unique appearance, from the four white tunnels which rise some ten or twelve feet over the promenade deck, and which somewhat resemble Ionic pillars without the capital. They are thirty inches in diameter, and are supported by octagon pedestals, also white. Two of these columns, or pipes, carry off the air from the engine, and the other two servo as chimneys, l Around5 their tops, they are ornamented with gilt rings and mouldings. These gilt ornaments are now, after ten days tiring, perfectly bright. Entering the spar deck, the absence of any crank hatches, and a clear deck for two hundred leet on each side of the deck house, attract the eye. The berth deck likewise presents an unbroken line, with state rooms along the entire ship, and passages between the fore and aft saloons on both sides. As a model of naval architecture, there is not a vessel in our splendid merchant marine that can compete with the Ericsson for graceful proportions and symmetry of build. All who have seen her, concur in the expression

of admiration of litis beautiful ship, and in their opinion of her superior sailing qualities, independent of any aid from her machinery. For obvious reasons, those interested in the undertaking have observed great caution and jealousy to prevent any knowledge of the construction of Iter machinery See., from getting abroad. To guard against this, portions of it were made at various places- New York, Philadelphia, West Point, &c., from plans and specifications furnished by the inventor. i?o perfect and true were his calculations, that every piece of the machinery thus made lit tod in with the utmost exactitude so that, to give the language of one of the persons engaged in it, a sheet of tissue paper could not be put in between the joints. This circumstance, in itself, speaks well for the great engineering skill of its ! constructor. The same jealous caution was observed in permitting strangers on hoard. The exclusion of ali outsiders lias been very rigidly enforced, 60 that the hundreds whose cure sity brought them to visit her were forced to content themselves with a distant inspection. Thus, lias description of her up to the present time, no correct appeared in type ; and we therefore feel confident that that which we now present to our readers in relation to this remarkable vessel will be read with an interest proportionate to the importance of the invention, of which the Ericsson is the first embodiment. Let the reader, therefore, accompany us as we are chaperoned throughout the ship by her gailant and po-

lite commander, Capt. A. B. Lowber, to whose ability and experience as a navigator she lias been well confided. Let me first show you, says c.nr guide, the freight deck and then we will ascend and examine her in detail. To the height deck, therefore, we descended, and were pointed out its great capacity, extending as it does some 260 feet. It is entirely free from obstruction o! every kind, excepting only a space along the , middle which contains the cylinders, enclosed within strong bulkheads. None of its room is to be devoted, as in steamers to the carrying of coal, which is stowed away in sufficient quantity, each side of the engine. It is calculated thus to carry 1,400 tons of teas, or other light merchandize, or it engaged in the Australia or Cali lornia trade, it is well adapted for accommodating some tour or five bunded passengers. A ventilator, on a new principle and connected with the machinery, extends to this deck. About midships there is a sort of square enclosure, which, vve learned, communicated only with the main deck, and which has been fitted This lor Hie female servants ol the cabin passengers. up is a great improvement on the present plan, which makes little or no provision for this class of travellers. VVc found this room neatly and comfortably furnished, with twelve or fourteen berths, and conveniences for bandboxes and the various et ceteras of waiting women. (To bo continued.)

The þÿPresident Message. s The document was transmitted to Congress on Monday, soon after the assembling of the two Houses. It is moderate in length, and equally moderate in every other respect. J\o one expected anything of importance or force to be said in it, and so no one has I been disappointed. The following are the passages that will most interest our readers : The Fisheries. In the course of the last summer considerable anxiety was caused for a short time by an official intimation from the government of Great Britain that orders had been given lor the protection of the fisheries upon the coasts of the British provinces in North America against the alleged encroachments of the fishing vessels of the United States and France. The shortness of this notice and the. season of the year seemed to make it a matter of urgent importance It was at first apprehended that an increased naval force had been ordered to the fishing grounds to carry into effect the British interpretation of those provisions in the convention of 18J8, in reference to the true intent of which the two governments differ. It was soon discovered that such was not the design of Great Britain, and satisfactory explanations of the real objects of the measure have been given both here and in London. The unadjusted difference, however, between the two governments as to the interpretation of the first article of the convention of 1818 is still a matter of importance. American fishing vessels within nine or ten years have been ex-

cluded from waters to which they had free access for 2» years after the negociation of the treaty. In 1845 the exclusion was relaxed so far as concerns the Bay of Fundy, but the just and liberal intention of the Home government, in compliance with what we think the true j become construction of the convention, to open all the outer bays to our fishermen, was abandoned, in consequence of the opposition of the colonies. Notwithstanding this, the United States have, since

fishermen in 1845, pursued the most liberal course toward the colonial fishing interests. By the revenue law of 1846, the duties on colonial fish entering our ports were very greatly reduced, and by the warehousing act it is allowed to be entered in bond without payment of duty. In this way colonial fish has acquired the monopoly of the export trade in our market, and is entering to some extent into the home consumption. These facts were among those which increased the sensibility of our fishing interest, at the movement in question. Thesucircumstances and the incidents above alluded to have led me to think the moment favorable for a reconsideration of the entire subject of the fisheries on the coast of the British provinces, with a view to place them upon a more liberal footing of reciprocal privilege. A willingness to meet us in some arrangement of this kind is understood to exist, on the part ot Great Britain, with a desire on her part to include in one comprehensive settlement, as well this subject as the commercial intercourse between the United States and the British provinces. I have thought that whatever arrangements may be made on these two subjects, it is expedient that they should be embraced in separate conventions. The illness and death of the late Secretary of State prevented the commencement of the contemplated negotiation. Pains have been taken to col-

OSOIZ 4T 1 3 | lect the information required for the details of such an arrangement. The subject is attended with considerable difficulty. If it is found practicable to come to an agreement mutually acceptable to the two parties, conventions may be concluded in the course of the present winter. The control of Congress over all the provisions of such an arrangement, affecting the revenue, will of course be reserved.

Cuba. The affairs of Cuba formed a prominent topic in my last annual message. They remain in uneasy condition, and a feeling of alarm and irritation on the part of the Cuban authorities appears to exist. This feeling has interfered with the regular commercial intercourse between the United States and the island, and led to some acts of which we have a right to complain. But the Captain General of Cuba is clothed with no power to treat with foreign governments, nor is he in any degree under the control of the Spanish Minister at Washington. Any communication which he may hold with an agent of a foreign power is informal and matter of courtesy. Anxious to put an end to the existing inconveniences, (which seem to rest on a misconception,) I directed the newly-appointed Minister to Mexico to visit Havana, on his way to Vera Cruz. He was respectfully received by the Captain General, who conferred with him freely on the recent occurrences ; but no permanent arrangement was effected. In the meantime, the refusal of the Captain General to allow passengers and the mail to be landed in certain cases, lor a reason which does not furnish in the opinion of this Government even a good presumptive ground for such a prohibition, has been made the subject of a serious remonstrance at Madrid ; and I have no reason to doubt that due respect will be paid by the Government of Her Catholic Majesty to the representations which ot:r Minister has been instructed to make on the subject. It is but justice to the Captain General to add,

that his conduct toward the steamers employed to carry the mails of the Iiited States to Havana has, with the exceptions above allud. d to, been marked with kindness and liberality, and indicate s no general purpose of interfering with the commercial correspondence and intercourse between the island and this country. Early in the present year official notes were received from the Minister of France and England, inviting the Government of the United States to a party with Great Britain and France, to a tripartite Convention, in virtue of which the three powers should severally and collectively disclaim, now and for the future, all intention to obtain possession of the T-dand of Cuba, and should bind themselves to discountenance all atthe Bay of Fundv was re-opened to our I tempts to that effect on the part of any power or individual whatever. This invitation has been respectfully declined, for reasons which it would occupy too much space in this communication to state in detail, but which led mo to think that the proposed measure would be of doubtful constitutionality, impolitic, and unavailing. I have, however, in common with several of my predecessors, directed the Ministers of France and England to be assured that the United States entertain no designs against Cuba; but that, on the contrary, I should regard its incorporation into the Union at the present time as fraught with serious peril. Were this island comparatively destitute of inhabitants, or occupied by a kindred race, 1

should regard it, if voluntarily ceded by Spain, as a most desirable acquisition. But, under existing circumstances, I should look upon its incorporation into our Union as a very hazardous measure. It would bring into the Confederacy a population of a different national stock, speaking a different language, and not likely to harmonise with the other members. It would probably affect in a prejudicial manner the industrial interests of the South ; and it might revive those conflicts of opinion between the different sections of the country, which lately shook the Union to its centre, and which have been so happily compromised.

tingelser tor Samfundsforholdene, soni kun ere heregnede paa at skaffe Borgerne den fornodne Sikkerhed. At denne betryggende Deel at Lovgivningen, ved en undernaervaerende Omstaendighederemani rende ny yEgteskahs-Lov, kaldes i Vedkommendes Erindring og bekjendtgjores som vedhli vende at skulle hestaae, anseer Minoriteten paa Grund afdet ovenan forte som nodvendigt. Fremdeles skal Minoriteten tillade sig at ben.ocrke folgende. Med Ilensyn til .Egteskaber imellem Lutheranere og Tilhaengere af den romerske Tro, bestemte Loven hidtil, at Revers skulde udstaedes for Bornenes Opdragelse i den lutherske Tro (jvfr. Frd. 30te Apr. 1824 13), samt at Vieisen skal forrettes af den lutherske Praest, hvad enten Bruden ! eller Brudgommen er Lutheraner (jvfr. Ilescr. 6te Sept. 1690, samt Frd. 30te Apr. 1824 14). Det er, som ovenfor i bemaerket, vel ikke klart, hvorvidt omhandlede tvende Paragrapher 8 <fc 9, h vis de udvidedeshertil, vilde angaae Lutheranere og saaledes opbaeve disse hidtil gjaeldende Bestemmelser. For det mulige Tilfaeldes Sky Id, at dette kunde saettes igjennem, fortjenerdot formeentlig at paaagtes, at dcrsom Bestemmelsen om Udstacdelsen af Revers ophaeves, da ma a dette, som Gouvernementet i sine Motiver til dette Lovudkast har beniaerket, « ansces at vaere en af Tidens Fordringer, at dette Baand bortfalder." Derimod f'orholder det sig efter Minoritetens Formening anderledes med Bestemmelsen om, at den lutherske Praest forretter Vieisen, hvad enten Bruden

eller Brudgommen er Lutheraner. Det hor her formeentlig komme i Betragtning, at den romerske Kirke ikke skjienker nogensomhelst nrotestantisk Vielse sin kirkelige Anerkjendelse, ihvorvel den muligviis tilstaaer protestantiske Vielser en saakaldet horgerlig eller lovlig Anerkjendelse. Den romerske Kirkes Functioner ansee sig desaarsag pfigtige til at forrette enhver protesfantisk Vielse om igjen. Derimod skjaenke de protestantiske Kirker en romersk Vielse ligesaa fuldelig Anerkjendelse som en protestantisk Vielse Den hidtil gjaeldende Bestemmelse, at Vieisen imellem en Lutheraner og en Tilhaenger af den romerske Tro altid tilfalder den lutherske Preest er ikke nogen Forret for den Intherskc Kirke. Forholdet imellem den lutherske og romerske Kirke er ved denne Bestemmelse kun stillet lige, idet den lutherske Vielse gjentages af den romerske Praest, en romersk Vielse derimod anerkjendes af Lutheranere. þÿ Saafremt altsaa ogsaa skulle omfatte Folkekirken, saa burde en Tilfoielse i alt Fald vaere skeet til naevnte 8, saa at den berorte Bestemmelse af Frdn. 30te Apr. 1-24 % 14 forbliver uophaevet. Fremdeles hor det formeentlig komme i Betragtning, at de ovrige protestantiske Kirker ere i naevnte Henseende lige Vilkaar undergivne som den lutherske Kirke. De anerkjende nemlig, som ovenfor anfort, den romerske Praests Vielser; han derimod underkjender den kirkelige Betydning af deres V'ielses-Handlinger og forretter samnie om igjen. Da dette er saa, vil nodvendigviis de

forskjellige anerkjendte Troessamfunds ligelige Stilling i Forhold til hverandre behove en Stotte i heskjsermende Forskrivter fra StatensSide. En indbyrdes Ligelighed imellem dem synes at vaere en passende Gjenstand for Lovgiverens, omendog skaansomme Tilsyn ; t hi det vil vaere vanskeligt at give Ordet Religionsfrihed en sand Betydning, naar den ei er forenet med en indhvrdes ligelig Stilling imellem de forskjaellige Troessamfund. Man kan ikke forhyue den romerske Prsest at forrette den protestantiske Vielse om igjen, ligesaalidet som

man kunde byde ham at skjnenke sandan Vielse hans kirkelige Anerkjendelse. Der staaer da formeentlig ene tilbage, at Lovgiveren tilkjender den protestaritiske Prsest at forrette Vielsen for den rumerske Prsest. Lovgiveren kan med Ilensyn til de anerkjendte Troessamftinds ligelige Stilling ingenlunde blive staaendc ved den blot negative Bestemmelse, at " Ingen kan paa Grand af sin Troesbekjendelse beroves Adgang til den fnlde Nydelse af borgerlige og politiske Retligbeder o. s. v." (see Damn. Riges Grundlov 84.) Men ligesom desaarsag Grundlovens83 tilsiger, at disse "Troessamfnnds Forhold mermere skulle ordnes ved Lov," saaledes bar de protestantiske Kirkers ligelige Stilling nied den romerske i omrorte lienseende formeentlig naermest Krav paa Lovgiverens Opal aerksomhed.
