m IB I & I SP© HIS MAJESTY the KING concerning flic extension to the Danish Wcwtinriia Possessions ot paragraphs 8 and 1) of flic Law of IBlli April 1851, relative fo marriages hetxveen members of different religions persuasions. Concluded. There is another circumstance which ought to be taken into consideration, namely that whereas it is regulated that a law issued in Denmaik, shall be examined here, whether it is applicable to the colony or not, thus the object of this regulation no doubt must be to advance and politically to develop the legislation of the colonies in an equal degree w ith that of the mother country. Such an examination, the minority think, ought to have been made with the whole law in question, and not limited to a part thereof. The enquiry ought to have been, whether civil marriages as ordered and regulated by the law in question, are advisible here in the colonv. By deviating from such a manner of proceeding the enquiry was rendered unsettled ai d insufficient; a totally different question from what by just usage and practice might have been expected, was brought under discussion ; this namely has been the subject bofore the council, whether a small fragment of the law in question could be altered thus as to render an extension to the colonies possible. Such a manner of proceeding must lead to an uncertain result and is at all events, we think, out of the regular way. By this means and in the present case it is a real nuisance that laws of the mother conn

try are to be examined for extension to these parts. Fof if Ibis were not so, a better and more judicious plan of legislation would have been adopted in order to make a new mar riage-law. As was done with respect to the labour-law, servants law and other drafts of laws laid before the council, thus also in this case notice would have been taken of customs prevalent here, and it would have been tried, which of these customs could be sane tioned as legal ; the regulations also, hilheita valid here, would have been examined, w hich now are left unexamined and undiscussed ; circumstances and habitudes extant bete would have been taken into consideration, which now have been, partly at least, unno ticed. We regret the mariner of proceeding that has been used; for as in all cases thus also in this the draft of law, that was laid before the council to be discussed, there must have and has had an essential influence on the issue of the debate and the contents of the report. Amendments proposed during the discussion, may compensate for some of the defects in the original draft. This we will not deny. But it is not likely, that a draft labouring under essential deficiencies and wants, will through the means of amendments have such imperfections remedied. Nor do we think that the majority of the Council have succeeded in their attempt as to the present case. It was alleged during the discussions that the old regulations about marriage should be

considered as valid and continue in force, in so far as they do not militate against the proposed new law. It must be observed, liuwever, that though such a compromise between old laws and a new one is applicable no doubt, when those officials, to whom it is left to carry out the laws and enact the regulations, are lawyers, and thereby capacitated to interpret the laws, yet this can hardly be done in the present case. For it ought to be remembered, that the greater part of the clergy in the colonies being front Germany, England or North America, do rately during their sojourn here become acquainted with Danish language, literature or interpretation of laws If then it is moreover considered, that the representative institution now granted these islands in the Colonial Council is with regard to the framing of laws a new period, different from the foregoing time in so far as drafts of laws are now made known also to those inhabitants who do not speak Danish, which was not the case formerly, if this is considered, we say, it will no doubt be granted, that it cannot be sufficient to supply the defects of the present draft of law from the old marriage-laws; for these laws are hardly known to the neater part of the clergy, and the compatibility or incompatibility of the old laws with the new one is n subject not easily dtjudioaied. The marriage-regulations that obtain here, contain, we will not deny, some limitations, which might without any risk he abolished But when it is regarded, how much the rights

of parents and guardians may fie encroached upon, and how much injustice towards an individual may lie committed by nn uncontrolled liberty of forming marriages, then a glance at the hitherto availing mairiugc-laws will convince any one that n not inconsiderable part of those laws are calculated to procure tire citizens some necessary security. In case now a new law shall be issued, the majority thinks it necessary, that this part of the older laws should be published as valid also in future. Furtheimore the minority shall lake the liberty to make the following observation. With regard to marriages between Lutherans and Romans the law hitherto prescribed, that a reverse should be signed for the children to be brought up in the Lutheran persuasion (cfr. ordinance 30th April 1824 paragraph 13) ; and the law likewise prescribed, that the wedding shall be performed by the Lutheran minister, whether the bride or the bridegroom is a Lutheran (see rescript fltli September 1000, and ordinance 80lh April 1824 paragraph 14) Now it is not clear, as rentai ked above, that these two regulations will be affected or altered by an eventual extension to these pails of paragraphs 8 and 9, since these paragraphs do m>t perhaps concern tnembeis of the i ational Church. In case, however, said regulations were abolished, we shall not omit here to repeat an opinion expressed by Government in the preamble of the dralt concerning the first-mentioned regulation, that it considers the reverse as a

limitation which the present time calls for being discontinued. But as for tiie regulation that the Lutheran minister shall peifotm the wedding whether the bride or the bridegroom is a Lutheran, lite case is according to the opinion of the minority a different one. It ought fiere to bo taken into consideration, that the Roman church docs not grant to nnv prutestant marriage whatever, her ecclesiastical acknowledgment, although perhaps she may allow protestant marriages a sort of civil or so called legal acknowledgment The functionaries of the Roman church, therefore, consider themselves undet obligation to perform any protestant marriage over again. On the other hand the protcstant churches as fully acknowledge a Roman as a protestanl marriage. The regulation hitherto obtaining, that the marriage between a Lutheran and a Roman (Jatholic is first to be performed by the Lutheran minister, is not any prerogative on the part of the Lutheran church. The two churches are by this regulation only placed on a scale of equality, since, as observed, the Lutheran marriage is performed over again by the Roman priest, while a

Roman marriage is acknowledged by the Lutherans. In case, therefore, the law also comprehends the Lutherans, an addition ought to be made to the 8th paragraph, so that the regulation of 30ih April 1824 paragraph 14, as mentioned above, be not by the paragraph annulled. It ought, we think, furthermore be considered, that the other protestant churches are in said respect situated equally with the Lutheran church. Acknowledging, as above observed, the marriages performed by the Roman priest, their marriages, not having the ecclesiastical acknowledgment of the Roman church, are by the priest thereof performed over again. It seems then, that the different acknowledged persuasions will necessarily require some defensive regulations on the part of the State as to how they stand equally connected with each other. This connection of equality seems to be a proper subject of oversight, though lenient of course, on the part of the lawgiver ; " for it would bo difficult to give to the word religious liberty" its full and true signification, if not combined with mutual equality ninong the different persuasions. The Roman priest cannot be prohibited from performing over again a protestant marriage; no more than he can be enjoined to confer to such a union his ecclesiastical avowal of its validity. Nothing then remains but for the lawgiver to grant the protestant clergyman a right of first marrying the couple in question. As to the equal position of the acknowledged persuasions, the lawgiver cannot con-

tent himself with a merely negative regulation as the one found in the fundamental law paragraph 84. that " no one can he excluded, on account of his religious profession, from the full enjoyment of civil and political rights &c." But forasmuch as the 83rd paragraph doe3 in consequence appoint " a future regulation by iaw of the concerns of such persuasions," thus an equal position between the Roman and Protestant churches in said respect has undoubtedly a claim on the attention of the lawgiver. Whereas the paragraphs, even in their amended shape, would not secure to the protestant churches, nay perhaps not even to the national church such an equal position with the Roman, this one reason more for the minority to disrecommend the extension of said paragraphs. The law of 13th April 1851 was given at a time, when the minds of the people were distracted with many doubts, and the object of the law was, as it seems, to becalm the loudest clamours about expected freedom from restrictive regulations concerning the church. This law, therefore, is not without traces of that disquietude and uncertainty, during which it came into existence; and even the short time that has elapsed since then has been sutficiently long for some of its deficiencies to be discovered. But now to extend to these islands a dismembered fragment of such a law, that was called into existence by a momentary, evanescent demand, that was given for a community highly different from ours both in other respects and

also in regard of church- matters and religion, this is in our opinion a hazardous undertaking. In the parent-country there are hitherto only few members of the acknowledged persuasions. The defects of tiie law may in consequence there only appear singly and unnoticed ; the evils derived from it may be few in number and not much known. But here a belong to ' different acknowledged persua- much larger proportion of t tie inhabitants sions and if the paragraphs were introduced here as laws, they would of course have greater influence arid more extensive efficacy. From the rensons allcdged above, the minority must dissuade the extension to the Danish Westindian Possessions of paragraphs 8 and 9 of the law about marriage 1 3th April 1851. Thus we transmit this our most submissive report.

The Caloric Ship llricNNon. (Concluded.) From the freight deck we ascend by a wide stairway to the main deck. This is occupied from stem to stern by sixty state rooms ; those in the aft cabin fitted up with two berths each, and those in the forward cabin with three. We inspected the latter portion first, and were struck with the elegance and taste with which it was fitted up. We were immediately reminded of the motto which wo saw in a conspicuous position 011 board þÿ "Everything in its place, and a place for everything" þÿ and we felt the conviction that this maxim was not lost sight of in the construction and fitting up of the ship. The state rooms communicate direct with the saloon by a gotliic arched door, which opens on j every two rooms. They are richly carpeted, and are lighted by day with deck and side lights, and by night with a three-sided lamp, so fitted in the panuelling as to furnish a light at the same time to two rooms and the saloon. These lamps are provided with a lock, and are to be in charge of one of the employees. The berths are handsomely fitted up; the matresses are composed of the best curled hair; and the bedclothes -are also of the whitest and finest texture, and marked with the word Ericsson in red letters. A marble-slab wash basin and appurtenances belong to each room ; and on the side opposite the berths is a sort of day sofa, which answers the very necessary use of a receptacle for soiled clothes and boots. A small bronze framed mirror, with a pivot which permits it to be turned in

every direction, completes the furniture of these apartments. W e must not forget to mention that a fine room is also fitted up here for the accommodation of the waiters connected with the vessel, who are obliged, on other ships, to stow themselves away under the tables and elsewhere. Fourteen double berths are provided for them, and all the conveniences of water pipes, wash basins, mirrors, &c. The forward cabin saloon is very handsomely furnished and presents a chaste appearance, from the gothic style of the doors, which open into the state rooms, and from its general decorations. The chairs and sofas are covered with crimson plush, and are of the neatest pattern. The carpets are of a very rich and beautiful material, the design representing the American flag interspersed with forest foliage, Sic. The panels are painted white, shaded with a light tinge of purple, and decorated with gilding. The device round the cornices, on raised gilded work, represents Neptune in his chariot, drawn by sea monsters. In fact, the only point of distinction between the aft and forward cabins, is, that the rooms of the latter are fitted up with an extra berth ; and if it were judged advisab'c to have a uniformity of price for passage, the plan could be easily carried into execution, it being only requisite to take "away the third berth from each of the forward cabin state rooms. For the saloon there is a steward's pantry amidships, provided with neat delpb, glass, cutlery, &c., and communicating by a dumb waiter

with the kitchen. The state rooms of the after cabin, which is merely separated from the other by passage doors, are in no respect different, except in the number of berths, from those we have just described. They range along each side of the deck, the central space being occupied with the machinery, to which several doors admit an entrance. These doors have a circular pane of glass to allow passengers to witness the working of the machinery. A barber shop is fitted up in the state room through which the shaft runs, the corresponding room on the opposite side being used as a store room. The saloon is larger and furnished perhaps in a more expensive style than the forward cabin, hut the character of the furniture and fittings is precisely the same. This saloon is heated by a hot air apparatus, and ventilated by the same means as is the freight deck, except that here the ventilator is shut in by a stained glass frame Hot and cold air can be supplied to any part of the vessel from the engine. The peculiar construction of the ship, and comparatively small room occupied by the machinery afford an inner promenade round the whole course of the cabins, extending some five hundred feet. On the upper deck the space between tire cabins and the side of the vessel, is some twelve feet wide, extending also round the ship. The ladies' boudoir in the after cabin, is a handsome semicircular apartment, furnished with great elegance, and richly carpeted. It is entered from the main saloon by two doors on opposite sides ; round the bend

of the room a sofa is arranged with a marble slab table in front of it. There are besides in the room several ottomans and luxurious arm chairs, covered witli ricli crimson plush, and the walls are ornamented with mirrors. There is also a neat library fitted up in this room, with mirror doors, the lower part of it being reserved for a medicine chest. The apartment is one of the most chaste and elegant we have ever seen assigned to the purpose in a ship. From the main cabin there are four stairways to the upper deck. Here is the dining hall for the aft cabin passengers. This is a fine well lighted room, painted in imitation of oak, having mirrors and windows in each alternate sections of panels. There are several book cases in the room, which is also supplied with comfortable sofas. Leading from it forward, we come upon a small circular apartment, containing a glass case for the ship's plate, &c., and here, also, is the main pantry, a room for the storekeeper to issue wine, and a water tank with filter, capable of holding one hundred and five gallons. The remainder of this deck, forward, isoccupied in kitchen, steward's rooms, officors' mess, &.c. ; and aft is a smoking room for the first Cabin passengers, with a fine comtortablc wheel house in which is a place for stowing ammunition, &c. One of the greatest peculiarities in the fitting up of this ship is the absence of all angularities, and one cannot but admire the skill with which every available

3 3F G Ui D 4TI spot is adapted to the best use, while all arrangements are of the most regular kind. Nor in the attention to the comfort of the passengers has the comfort and well being of the sailors and firemen been overlooked þÿ the forecastle is neatly fitted up with berths, water pipes, i gelige Bogholder-Contoirer paa St. Croix og St. Thobasins, mirrors, library, &c., and 011 the larboard side the like accommodations have been provided for the firemen. Having arrived thus far in our gratifying inspection of the Ericsson, we were led to that portion assigned to the machinery. This part is characterized by the same neatness, and exhibits the same proofs of superior skill and management as are observable throughout every other part of it. Apart from the main principle, the distinguishing feature of the engines of the Ericsson consist in dispensing with the centre shaft, whilst at the same time two pairs of working cylinders are employed, imparting a continuous rotary movement, as in the double marine steam engine. The arrangement by which Captain Ericsson attains this desirable uniform action presents one of the most elegant mechanical combinations ever produced. Each pair of working cylinders, with their appropriate supply cylinders, are placed parallel to the ship's centre line; one pair forward of, and the other abaft the paddie shaft. The supply cylinders being inverted and placed at some distance above the working cylinders, with their open ends presented to the open ends of the work-

ing cylinders, a space is formed between the two, which contains a triangular lever for transmitting the vertical energy of the working pistons to the crank of the paddle shaft by a diagonal movement. The mean angle of their diagonal being about forty five degrees abaft the vertical plane of the paddle shaft, in the aft engine, and forty five degrees forward of that plane in the forward engine, it is obvious that the forces of the two engines will be exerted nearly at right angles to each other. Hence the double cranks, and the objectionable centre shaft of the marine steam engine, are obviated, a single crank placed in the middle of the caloric ship serving to transmit, in a perfect manner, the continuous rotary motion required in turning paddle wheels for ocean purpose. In further comparing the machinery of the Ericsson with the double marine steam engine, it will be found that the four sida levers have disappeared; the cross heads and cross tails likewise; nor are the four side rods to be found; and, above all, the absence of the parallel motion, with their nicely adjusted joints, and levers for converting the curved movements into straight ones, claim attention In place of all these parts will be found simply a triangular lever for each engine, with a link and connecting rod for transmitting the power of the pistons to the crank of the paddie shaft. Again, the four huge boilers of the ocean steamer give place to tour small furnaces, erected under the working cylinders. Force

pumps, brine pump, safety valves. &e., and the network of connecting pipes, which fill the bottom of the ocean steamer, have all disappeared ; and in place of gaugccocks, brine gauges, injection valves, Sic , Si c., calling for incessant vigilance on the part of many minds and hands at once, a single handle attached to the valve gear of the engines, regulates at the will of a single mind, the movements of a caloric ship. Starting, stopping, backing and checking being effected by this single handle, without any regard to particular conditions, so essential in working tne engines of the ocean steamer. The arrangement of the caloric ship being such tiiat the required air for the engines þÿ from 50 to 70 tons weight per þÿhour has to pass through the fiie rooms before entering the supply cylinders, it has been found in the Ericsson that the temperature is actually too low for the comfort of the firemen. Aa an engineering achievement, the machinery of the Ericsson is very far aiiead of anything afloat. The engineer who beholds four open cylinders, each of 168 inches in diameter, with their pistons of upwards of twenty two thousand superficial inches area, moving up and down in sight, through a space of six feet, can best appreciate the greatness of tiiat achievement. To the ordinary observer the movement of the whole machine is wonderful. And we cannot but feel extremely gratified that tnc caloric principle was introduced to the world on a scale so commensurate with its impor-
tance, and that our metropolis lias the honor of initiating it.
